《耶鲁开放课程系列》旨在将耶鲁教育的深度和广度带给广大读者。该系列丛书以耶鲁大学开放课程项目（http://oyc.yale.edu）为基础，汇集了耶鲁大学教授的精彩讲座，供求知欲强的读者（无论学生还是成人）阅读。涵盖社会科学、自然科学和人文科学等多个学科的广泛主题，《耶鲁开放课程系列》丛书以经济实惠的价格提供易于理解的入门读物。

THE OPEN YALE COURSES SERIES is designed to bring the depth and breadth of a Yale education to a wide variety of readers. Based on Yale’s Open Yale Courses program (http://oyc.yale.edu), these books bring outstanding lectures by Yale faculty to the curious reader, whether student or adult. Covering a wide variety of topics across disciplines in the social sciences, physical sciences, and humanities, Open Yale Courses books offer accessible introductions at affordable prices.

前言

Preface

这些章节的出版过程可谓非同寻常，不过本书所属的丛书或许会改变这一现状。2009年春季学期，我在耶鲁大学开放课程“文学300”中讲授了26节课，这些课都被录像了，但你也可以在上班路上或跑步时收听录音。考虑到文字稿可能也同样受欢迎，于是便开始了最终演变成本书的过程。这些讲座都是我即兴发挥的，每节课都只用一页左右的笔记作为参考。录音带被寄往圣地亚哥，由一台机器记录下它听到的内容。之后，机器将记录结果交给纽黑文的一位编辑，由她进行整理和润色。当时我本应该像过去几个月那样去做，但那时动力太低，我只是匆匆浏览了一下笔录，做了一些快速的修改——尽管我意识到书面记录看起来就像一个笑话，或者像是经过太多人之手流传的八卦。

These chapters have passed through transformations that must be unusual in publishing, although the series the book appears in will probably change that. My twenty-six Open Yale Courses lectures in “Lit 300” for the Spring 2009 semester were videotaped, yes, but you could hear them as audiotape, too—while driving to work or going for a run—and on the assumption that the written transcripts might also appeal, the process then began that morphed at last into the written form of this book. I had delivered the lectures extemporaneously, guided for each one by a page or so of scribbled notes. The audiotape was sent to San Diego, where a machine wrote down what it thought it heard. The result was then given to a human being in New Haven who made what she could of it. That was the point at which I should have done what I’ve been doing for the last several months, but the incentive was then too low, and I took time only to glance through the transcripts and make a few quick changes—despite realizing that the written record was getting to look like a joke or a bit of gossip that has passed through too many hands.

从某种意义上说，当时不做任何改动似乎也合情合理，因为这些原本应该是文字稿，而不是改写稿。尽管它们的准确度堪比电视上为听障人士提供的即时字幕，但谁也无法断言有人故意做了任何修改。不过，现在它们即将结集出版：当然，既有电子版也有纸质版，但终究是一本书。耶鲁大学出版社的一位编辑在收到文字稿后立即进行了润色。之后，讲稿以压缩文件的形式发送给了我，标记编辑程序已经预先激活，我便开始着手编辑。这时，我一直在思考一篇我为这门课布置的著名且出了名的晦涩难懂的文章（第十三章会讨论到）的开头几段，那就是雅克·拉康的《无意识中的文字能动性》。拉康说，他的论文是研讨会演讲的书面版本（收录于名为《文集》的文集中）。他认为，若要充分表达他对语言在无意识中作用的论述，就必须保留当时的口语语境。同时（尽管拉康并未明言），任何有聆听经验的读者都显而易见：自发性口语中传递的信息或许足以应对当时的场合，但当读者以更为悠闲的注意力阅读书面文本时，这些信息的接收方式却截然不同。因此，鉴于本书是为读者而作，我修改了讲座中我认为需要更细致阐述的部分，同时力求保留讲座原有的语调。众所周知，我即兴发挥时常使用“散文式”语言，所以当您遇到长句时，请不要以为它在讲座中就更短。

In a way it then made sense to leave it alone, though, because these were supposed to be transcripts, not rewrites, and even though they had the accuracy of those instant captions for the hearing-impaired on television, nobody could say that any changes had intentionally been made. They are now to become a book, however: both digital and print, to be sure, but still a book. An editor at Yale University Press took the transcript in hand on first receiving it and made some cosmetic improvements. The lectures were then sent to me as a zip-file, the mark-up editing program already activated, and I went to work. At this point, I kept thinking about the first few paragraphs of a famous and famously difficult essay that I’d assigned for the course (discussed in Chapter 13), Jacques Lacan’s “Agency of the Letter in the Unconscious.” His paper, he says, is a written version (écrit, in a volume called Écrits) of a seminar presentation. He feels that the orality of that occasion is important to retain if he is to convey to the fullest what he wants to say about the role of language in the unconscious. At the same time (though Lacan doesn’t say this), it’s quite obvious to any reader with experience as a listener that information conveyed in spontaneous speech is perhaps adequate to its occasion but not registered in at all the same way when it’s taken in during a reader’s more leisurely focus on a written text. Because this book is for readers, therefore, I have modified such parts of the lectures as seemed to me to need a more careful exposition, while hoping to retain a sense throughout of what the lectures sounded like. I am, notoriously, an impromptu speaker of “prose,” so when you encounter a long sentence, please don’t think it was any shorter in the lecture.

如果没有我的助手斯特凡·埃斯波西托（Stefan Esposito）的大力协助，我根本无法专注于应对我之前描述的那项意料之外的挑战。斯特凡是本次讲座录像的助教之一，也是比较文学领域一位重要的青年学者和理论家。我欣然委托他对所有章节进行最后的审阅和校对——每次我把稿件发给他时，邮件主题都写着“修订稿，第x号”。他撰写了书目论文《诠释的多样性》，并就我们讨论的每个主题提出了延伸阅读建议，这些建议将收录在本书末尾。他还提供了我们认为必要的参考文献（尽可能少），并将我曾在一些讲座上分发或发布在网上的讲义（包含待讨论的段落）整理成附录。

Without the extensive and indispensable help of my assistant, Stefan Esposito, I wouldn’t have been able to focus on the unexpected challenge I have described. Stefan was one of the teaching fellows for this videotaped version of the lectures and is an important emerging scholar and theorist in comparative literature. To him I happily entrusted a last read-through and correction of the chapters—for each of which my subject line was always “revised revision, #x”—when I sent them to him in Boston. He composed the bibliographical essay, “The Varieties of Interpretation,” with suggestions for further reading on each of our topics, which will be found at the end of the book. He has also furnished the references that we deemed necessary (as few as possible), and arranged in an appendix the handouts with passages to be discussed that I had circulated at some lectures or posted online.

尽管引用我布置的复印材料颇具挑战性，并且至少在某种程度上引入了我们原本希望避免的繁琐环节，但引用我们的主要教材却十分便捷。我强烈建议读者考虑购买这本优秀的著作，它在同类书籍中脱颖而出，其精选且丰富的材料（涵盖了批评史的方方面面）以及精辟的导论都令人印象深刻：戴维·里希特主编，《批评传统：经典文本与当代趋势》（第三版，波士顿：贝德福德/圣马丁出版社，2007）。所有引自该书的段落均在括号内注明出处，对应第三版。

Although references to the photocopied material I assigned have posed a challenge and at least conjecturally introduced a fussy element we had hoped in general to avoid, references to our main textbook were easy. I very strongly suggest that readers consider investing in this excellent volume, which stands out in the field for its judiciously and copiously chosen materials (including selections covering the entire history of criticism) and for its sensible introductions: David Richter, ed., The Critical Tradition: Classic Texts and Contemporary Trends (3rd ed.: Boston: Bedford/St. Martin’s, 2007). All quotations from that volume are keyed in parentheses to the third edition.

前两章是引言，包含了序言中常见的诸多歉意、免责声明和自夸，因此我在此就接下来对这一庞大主题的探讨内容不做过多赘述。不过，我意识到课程大纲并未涵盖某些近期颇具影响力的人物和思想，尽管文中偶尔会提及或预示这些趋势。例如，“伦理转向”涵盖了晚期德里达的思想，正如我所指出的，但我并未讨论乔治·阿甘本或雅克·朗西埃、阿兰·巴迪欧等新马克思主义者的作品。此外，英国马克思主义者对文本表面的关注也十分出色，西蒙·贾维斯、凯斯顿·萨瑟兰等人秉承创始人J·H·普林的精神进行微观阅读，而这种关注目前仅以他们才华横溢的学生的形式传入美国。

The first two chapters are introductory and offer a good many of the apologies, disclaimers, and boasts that one might expect to find in prefaces, so I shall say very little here about what the ensuing tour through this vast subject matter includes. I am conscious, however, that there are certain recently influential names and ideas that the syllabus did not stretch to cover, although here and there some oblique or proleptic mention of these trends will be found. The “ethical turn,” for example, encompasses late Derrida, as I point out, but I do not discuss the work of Giorgio Agamben or of neo-Marxists like Jacques Rancière and Alain Badiou. Also current is the brilliant Marxist attention devoted to textual surface in England, with Simon Jarvis, Keston Sutherland, and others micro-reading in the spirit of founder J. H. Prynne, which has only reached American shores as yet in the shape of their promising students.

文学社会学是一个新兴领域，但我对约翰·吉洛里（John Guillory）的讨论（以及在此背景下提及的皮埃尔·布迪厄）并未补充任何对社会语言学家迈克尔·西尔弗斯坦（Michael Silverstein）等重要著作的探讨。西尔弗斯坦的理论形成受到C.S.皮尔斯符号学的深刻影响；必须指出的是，随着克纳普（Knapp）和迈克尔斯（Michaels）（本文将对此进行讨论）等新实用主义观点与对文学知识和品味的社会文化传播的关注相融合，这种关注更多地借鉴了尤尔根·哈贝马斯（Jürgen Habermas）的“公共领域”概念，而非布迪厄的“惯习”（habitus）概念，一种类似于皮尔斯式的社会指示性符号传统已经出现，并与这些讲座主要关注的索绪尔传统形成竞争。目前尚未有关于皮尔斯传统的总体导论，我希望它能尽快问世。读者可以在我第二十五章的开头找到一些关于此主题的思考。

Literary sociology is an emerging field, but my discussion of John Guillory (and mention of Pierre Bourdieu in that context) is not supplemented by any discussion of the important work, for example, of the sociolinguist Michael Silverstein. A formative influence on Silverstein is the semiotics of C. S. Peirce; and it must be said that as neo-pragmatist views like those of Knapp and Michaels (discussed here) converge today with attention to the social and cultural circulation of literary knowledge and taste that is modeled on Jürgen Habermas’s concept of the “public sphere” even more than on Bourdieu’s concept of “habitus,” something like a Peirceian tradition of the socially indexical sign has emerged in rivalry with the Saussurian tradition to which these lectures devote most of their attention. A general introduction to the Peirceian tradition has yet to be written, and I hope it will quickly appear. The reader will find a few thoughts on this topic at the beginning of my twenty-fifth chapter.

除了本文讨论的福柯理论和文中顺带提及的安东尼奥·葛兰西理论之外，其他关于知识流通的理论近年来已将学者们引向系统理论（尤其是尼克拉斯·卢曼的理论）、媒体史、媒介重构和媒体理论（该领域的经典著作包括马歇尔·麦克卢汉和弗里德里希·基特勒的作品）等相互关联的领域，更具体地说，在这些领域中还包括书籍史（例如彼得·斯塔利布拉斯和大卫·卡斯坦的著作）。所有这些以及更多内容，都将在另一门课程和另一本书中进行探讨。

Theories of the circulation of knowledge other than those of Foucault, discussed here, and Antonio Gramsci, mentioned in passing, have recently carried scholars into the interrelated fields of systems theory (notably Niklas Luhmann), history of media, remediation, and media theory (the classics in this field being works by Marshall McLuhan and Friedrich Kittler), and more specifically within these last fields the history of the book (as in the work of Peter Stallybrass and David Kastan). All of this and more, then, remains to be covered in another course, and another book.

承认我的学术渊源——我指的是我个人的学术渊源，因为书面上的学术渊源大多都体现在书目论文中——是一项艰巨的任务。我在此仅列举几位多年来与我交谈和教导，无论他们是否意识到，都对我理解这一主题产生深远影响的人：杰弗里·亚历山大、约翰内斯·安德雷格、马歇尔·布朗、玛格丽特·弗格森、斯坦利·菲什、汉斯·弗雷、哈里斯·弗里德伯格、保罗·格里姆斯塔德、约翰·吉洛里、本杰明·哈沙夫、杰弗里·哈特曼、约翰·霍兰德、玛格丽特·霍曼斯、赫尔穆特·伊尔布鲁克、卡罗尔·雅各布斯、芭芭拉·约翰逊、杰里米·凯斯勒、埃里克·林德斯特罗姆、阿尔弗雷德·麦克亚当、大卫·马歇尔、欧文·马西、雷纳·内格勒、安娜·纳尔塞西安、爱德华·纳尔塞西安、西里尔·奥雷根、布里吉特·佩克、安东尼·里德、约瑟夫·罗奇、查尔斯·萨贝尔、娜奥米·肖尔、大卫·辛普森、彼得·斯塔利布拉斯、加勒特·斯图尔特、亨利·萨斯曼、史蒂夫·特德斯基、迈克尔·华纳，以及亨利·温菲尔德。比以往类似的情况更令我感到痛心，因为学习这些知识（以及接受教育）是一件至关重要却又微妙的事情。尽管我已经列出了一长串的致谢名单，但毫无疑问，我仍然遗漏了许多值得一提的人。我只能希望他们能庆幸自己没有因此受到牵连。我对我的教学伙伴们的感激之情，从我上世纪80年代第一次参与这门课程（当时保罗·德曼的学生们为我们的教学带来了他们的锐意和热情）开始，就铭刻在我的献词中。除了斯特凡·埃斯波西托之外，我还要感谢戴安娜·E·E·克莱纳（开放耶鲁课程的创始人和不知疲倦的支持者），以及耶鲁大学出版社的劳拉·达武利斯、克里斯蒂娜·塔克、索尼娅·香农、安妮-玛丽·伊姆博诺尼和阿尔多·库波，感谢他们一路以来的建议和鼓励。我还要感谢韦斯特切斯特图书集团的温迪·穆托和布莱恩·德斯蒙德，以及文字编辑朱莉·帕尔默-霍夫曼。

The challenge of acknowledging my intellectual debts—my personal ones, I mean, as the written ones find their way for the most part into the bibliographical essay—is overwhelming. I can name here only a few of the people whose conversation and teaching over the years have shaped my understanding of the subject, whether they knew it or not: Jeffrey Alexander, Johannes Anderegg, Marshall Brown, Margaret Ferguson, Stanley Fish, Hans Frei, Harris Friedberg, Paul Grimstad, John Guillory, Benjamin Harshav, Geoffrey Hartman, John Hollander, Margaret Homans, Helmut Illbruck, Carol Jacobs, Barbara Johnson, Jeremy Kessler, Eric Lindstrom, Alfred MacAdam, David Marshall, Irving Massey, Rainer Nägele, Ana Nersessian, Edward Nersessian, Cyril O’Regan, Brigitte Peucker, Anthony Reed, Joseph Roach, Charles Sabel, Naomi Schor, David Simpson, Peter Stallybrass, Garrett Stewart, Henry Sussman, Steve Tedeschi, Michael Warner, and Henry Weinfield. It pains me even more than it has on similar occasions in the past, educating oneself in these matters (and allowing oneself to be educated) being such a crucial yet delicate business, that despite having made what began to seem a rather long list of acknowledgments, I have undoubtedly forgotten so many who deserve a place on it. I can only hope they are relieved to have escaped guilt by association. My debt to my teaching fellows, from my first involvement with the course in the 1980s (when Paul de Man’s students brought their edge and zeal to our proceedings), is recorded in my dedication. For advice and encouragement along the way, in addition to Stefan Esposito I thank Diana E. E. Kleiner, the founder and tireless sustainer of Open Yale Courses, and, at Yale University Press, Laura Davulis, Christina Tucker, Sonia Shannon, Ann-Marie Imbornoni, and Aldo Cupo. My thanks also go to Wendy Muto and Brian Desmond at Westchester Book Group and to Julie Palmer-Hoffman, the copyeditor.

 

 

第一章

CHAPTER 1

介绍

Introduction

“理论”的史前史和兴起

The Prehistory and Rise of “Theory”

阅读材料：

Readings:

摘自马克思、尼采、弗洛伊德和保罗·利科的著作。

Passages from Marx, Nietzsche, Freud, and Paul Ricoeur.

首先，我想就我们课程的名称谈几点看法，因为它包含一些比较专业的词汇：“理论”和“文献”，这很显然，但“导论”这个词也值得一提。

Let me begin with a few remarks about the title of our course because it has some big words in it: “theory” and “literature,” clearly, but it’s worth saying something about the word “introduction” as well.

“理论”一词的词源历史十分复杂，我在此不赘述，仅指出其含义容易令人困惑之处。在某些时期，该词的实际用法使其类似于我们所说的“实践”，而在另一些时期，它的含义则与实践截然不同：它是一个可供实践应用的理念。后一种含义是如今“理论”一词的主流用法，但我们或许过于轻易地接受了它。对我们而言，理论与实践的区别不言而喻，但理论与方法论之间的区别却不那么明显。诚然，将方法论称为“应用理论”或许无可厚非，但这使其类似于实践——不妨称之为有条理的实践——正如我刚才所用的含义。而理论并非总是具有直接的应用价值。理论可以是一种纯粹的思辨性活动。它是一种关于某事物的假设，而我们未必需要确切地了解该事物的本质，因为理论本身就可能有助于揭示其本质。无论理论的对象是什么（如果它有对象的话），理论本身——由于可能存在的智力限制——比起特定的应用领域，更迫切地需要相当程度的内部一致性。

The word “theory” has a complicated etymological history that I won’t linger over except to point out what can make its meaning confusing. The way the word has actually been used at certain periods has made it mean something like what we call “practice,” whereas at other periods it has meant something very different from practice: a concept to which practice can appeal. This latter is the sense of theory that prevails today, but perhaps we accept it too quickly. Whereas for us the difference between theory and practice goes without saying, there’s a less obvious difference between theory and methodology. Yes, it’s probably fair enough to say that methodology is “applied theory,” but that makes it like practice—call it disciplined practice—in the sense I just used. Theory, on the other hand, does not always have an immediate application. Theory can be a purely speculative undertaking. It’s a hypothesis about something, the exact nature of which one needn’t necessarily have in view because theory itself may serve to bring it into view. Whatever the object of theory might be, if it even has one, theory itself requires—owing to whatever intellectual constraints may be in play—a large measure of internal coherence rather more urgently than a given field of application.

当然，大多数现有的理论形式都存在应用价值，这一点毋庸置疑。这类课程通常会选择一些文本作为例证——比如《利西达斯》、《古舟子咏》或一篇短篇小说——然后，讲座的讲解会不时暂停，文本会被拿出来，并将最近讨论过的理论应用于文本分析；因此，你可能会听到对《古舟子咏》的后殖民主义解读或创伤理论解读——顺便说一句，这方面有很多不错的解读——诸如此类，贯穿整个课程。

Of course there is no doubt that most existing forms of theory do exist to be applied. Very frequently, courses of this kind have a kind of proof text—Lycidas, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, a short story—and then once in a while the exposition of the lecture will pause, the text will be produced, and whatever type of theory has recently been talked about will be applied to the text; so that you’ll get a postcolonial reading or a trauma theory reading of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner—there have been a lot of good ones, by the way—and so on throughout the course.

虽然我不太愿意说理论应该总是有实际应用，尽管我知道通常情况下理论确实如此，但我不会打破这个惯例；不过，我会以一种略带敬意的方式，让它看起来，至少在某些时候，就像用轮子碾碎蝴蝶一样。我们今天的课文是一本幼儿故事书，叫做《拖车托尼》。这是一本用厚纸板做成的小书，每页底部都有一行文字，每页都画着一些表情各异的车辆，背景是一排房子，房子里的人脸或赞许或不赞许。我们暂时不会再用到这本书，但它篇幅很短，而且随着时间的推移，我们会用它做一些有趣的练习。当其他人重新研读《利西达斯》时，我们将重新回到《拖车托尼》，以此来引出一些应用理论的问题。

Now although I’m reluctant to say that theory should always have an application despite knowing that that’s what usually happens, I won’t depart from this custom; but I’ll poke a little respectful fun at it by making it seem, at least at times, like breaking a butterfly on a wheel. Our text is a story for toddlers called Tony the Tow Truck. It’s a little book made of thick cardboard pages with a line of text at the bottom, each page a picture of vehicles with human expressions and a row of houses with human faces expressing approval or disapproval in the background. We won’t come back to this text for a while, but it’s mercifully short, and as time passes we will do various tricks with it. As others revert to Lycidas, we shall revert to Tony the Tow Truck for the purpose of introducing questions of applied theory.

这种选择几乎丝毫没有对理论的轻蔑，更没有对文学文本的轻视。它更多的是提醒你，如果你能将理论应用于托尼，那么你就能将其应用于任何事物；同时也提醒你，阅读——阅读任何事物——毕竟是一项复杂且几乎无限的活动。这是理论教会我们最重要的道理之一，我希望能够在我们以各种方式解读拖车托尼的过程中证明这一点。

In this choice there is hardly any condescension toward theory and none at all toward literary texts. It’s much more a question of reminding you that if you can apply theory to Tony, you can apply it to anything; and also of reminding you that, after all, reading—reading just anything—is a complex and potentially almost unlimited activity. That’s one of the most important things that theory teaches us, and I hope to be able to prove it in the course of our varied approaches to Tony the Tow Truck.

理论与哲学，尤其是形而上学，或许在这一点上有些相似：它们都提出根本性问题，有时也构建体系。也就是说，理论旨在对可思考之物进行概括性的描述，这种描述与哲学相似，甚至与之匹敌。然而，二十世纪及以后的文学理论实践在大多数情况下与大多数哲学不同，因为它在很大程度上包含着怀疑主义。在文学理论中，似乎普遍存在着对我们思考基础的各种怀疑，而怀疑无疑也是其现代史的特征。并非本课程中阅读的所有理论都带有怀疑主义色彩。一些最有力、最深刻的文学理论思想，其意图和观点都是积极的，但总的来说，无论你是否乐意，你都将不得不接受这样一个事实：本课程推荐阅读材料中的许多内容都建立在，或者更确切地说，是受到这种持续存在的怀疑主义的制约。理论的怀疑精神至关重要，我以后还会反复谈到它，但现在我只是顺便提一下，为了唤起我们所谓的理论氛围。

Theory resembles philosophy, especially metaphysics, perhaps in this: it asks fundamental questions and also at times builds systems. That is to say, theory aims at a general description of what can be thought that resembles or rivals philosophy. But literary theory as practiced in the twentieth century and beyond differs in most instances from most philosophy in that to a surprising extent it entails skepticism. In literary theory there seems to be a pervasive variety of doubts about the foundations of what we can think, and it is certainly doubt that characterizes its modern history. Not all theory that we read in this course is skeptical. Some of the most powerful and profound thought that’s been devoted to the theory of literature is positive in its intentions and its views, but by and large you will be coming to terms—happily or unhappily—with the fact that much of what you’re going to find in the recommended readings accompanying this course is undergirded, or perhaps I should say undermined, by this persisting skepticism. It’s centrally important, the skepticism of theory, and I’m going to be coming back to it over and over, but now I mention it just in passing to evoke what we might call the atmosphere of theory.

说到“文学”这个词，这门课并非相对论、音乐理论或政府理论的课程，而是文学理论课程。文学理论与其他理论一样，都需要定义。或许理论提出的最根本、对我而言也可能是最引人入胜的问题就是：什么是文学？我们将要阅读的大部分内容都围绕这个问题展开，并为我们提供了引人入胜、且总是——各自独立——极具吸引力的定义。有些定义基于形式：循环性、对称性、形式的简洁性、形式的不简洁性以及重复。有些定义基于模仿：模仿“自然”、模仿心理或社会政治状态，这些定义诉诸于模仿的复杂性、平衡性、和谐性，有时也诉诸于不平衡和不和谐。还有一些定义坚持认为文学与其他类型的言语之间存在认识论上的区别：大多数言语都声称要表达关于世界实际状况的真理，而文学言语则没有这样的义务，这种观点认为，文学言语应该被恰当地理解为虚构——创造事物而不是指涉事物。

Turning to the word “literature,” this is not a course in theory of relativity, theory of music, or theory of government. This is a course in theory of literature, and theory of literature shares in common with other kinds of theory the need for definition. Maybe the most fundamental and, for me, possibly the most fascinating question theory asks is, what is literature? Much of what we’ll be reading takes up this question and provides us with fascinating and always—each in its turn—enticing definitions. There are definitions based on form: circularity, symmetry, economy of form, lack of economy of form, and repetition. There are definitions based on imitation: of “nature,” of psychological or sociopolitical states, definitions appealing to the complexity, balance, harmony, or sometimes imbalance and disharmony of the imitation. There are also definitions that insist on an epistemological difference between literature and other kinds of utterance: whereas most utterances purport to be saying something true about the actual state of things in the world, literary utterance is under no such obligation, the argument goes, and ought properly to be understood as fiction—making things rather than referring to things.

所有这些定义都曾流行过。我们会再次审视它们，并在深入了解的过程中发现它们各自的优点；但与此同时，即便我列举了这些可能性，你可能也在想，你很容易就能找到所有这些说法的例外。很好，这体现了你的包容精神，但与此同时，你的这种固执己见也让人感到不安，不是吗？也许文学根本就不是任何东西？ ——换句话说，文学或许无法被定义，无法被任何单一的定义所定义，它只是你认为它是什么，或者更准确地说，是你所在的阐释社群认为它是什么。但即便你得出这样的结论，只要你记住某些文学观念在某些社群中确实存在，这些观念本身就值得研究，而且毕竟你自己也完全清楚，并且在实际应用中也认同你的同伴们对文学的定义，那么它就不会显得那么令人沮丧。我刚才概述了所谓的文学新实用主义观点以及一般意义上的定义观，但这并不能成为我们不去界定研究对象的理由。定义对我们至关重要，即便它是暂时的，我们在本课程中也绝不会轻视它。

All of these definitions have had currency. We’ll be going over them again and discovering their respective merits as we learn more about them; but at the same time, even as I rattle off this list of possibilities, you’re probably thinking that you could easily find exceptions to all such claims. Well and good, that’s properly ecumenical of you, but at the same time your tough-mindedness raises the uneasy sense, does it not, that maybe literature just isn’t anything at all?—in other words, that literature may not be susceptible to definition, to any one definition, but is just whatever you think it is or, more precisely, whatever your interpretive community says that it is. But even if you reach that conclusion, it won’t seem disabling as long as you remember that certain notions of literature do exist in certain communities, that those notions in themselves reward study, and that after all you yourself know perfectly well, and for practical purposes agree with, what counts as literature among your peers. I have just outlined the so-called neo-pragmatist view of literature and of definition in general, but it doesn’t excuse us from delineating an object of study. Definition is important to us, even if it’s provisional, and we’re certainly not going to give it short shrift in this course.

除了定义文学之外，文学理论还会提出一些拓展这一领域的问题。文学的成因是什么？文学又会产生什么影响？关于成因，我们会问：什么是作者？文学权威的本质是什么？同样地，如果文学具有影响，它必然会对某些人产生影响，这就引出了一个同样有趣且令人困惑的问题：什么是读者？文学理论与这类问题密切相关，而对这些问题进行梳理的需求正是我们课程结构的基础。你会注意到，在这些讲座中，我们循序渐进地探讨了文学由语言构成、由人类心理构成以及由社会、经济和历史力量构成等观点。这些观点都与文学所产生的各种影响密切相关，而本课程也将按照同样的顺序逐一探讨这些推论。

In addition to defining literature, literary theory also asks questions that open up the field somewhat. What causes literature and what are the effects of literature? As to cause, we ask: What is an author? And what is the nature of literary authority? By the same token, if literature has effects, it must have effects on someone, and this gives rise to the equally interesting and vexing question, what is a reader? Literary theory is very much involved with questions of that kind, and the need to organize these questions is what rationalizes the structure of our course. You’ll notice from the contents that we move in these lectures from the idea that literature is formed by language to the idea that literature is formed by the human psyche to the idea that literature is formed by social, economic, and historical forces. There are corollaries for those ideas with respect to the kinds of effects that literature has, and the course moves through these corollaries in the same sequence.

最后，文学理论还提出了另一个重要的问题，我们将在探讨形式、心理和社会之前先从这个问题入手。这个问题与其说是“什么是读者？”，不如说是“阅读是如何进行的？”也就是说，我们——或者说任何人——如何得出结论，认为自己对文本的解读是恰当的，自己所进行的阅读是有依据的？阅读体验是怎样的？我们如何与文本面对面地交流？我们如何与文本建立联系，而文本在很多方面可能与我们相距甚远？这些问题正是诠释学所要探讨的，诠释学是一个晦涩难懂的词，我们稍后会详细解释。它源于赫尔墨斯神的名字，赫尔墨斯将语言传授给了人类，他也是沟通之神，身兼诸多职责。

Finally, literary theory asks one other important question, the one with which we’ll begin before turning to form, psyche, and society. This question is not so much “What is a reader?” but “How does reading get done?” That is to say, how do we—how does anyone—form the conclusion that we are interpreting something adequately, that we have a basis for the kind of reading that we’re doing? What is the reading experience like? How do we meet the text face-to-face? How do we put ourselves in touch with the text, which may in many ways be remote from us? These are the questions that are asked by what’s called hermeneutics, a difficult word that we will be taking up soon. It derives from the name of the god Hermes, who conveyed language to man and who was, among many other things, the god of communication.

以上就是关于文学及其理论语境的讨论。现在，我想就“导论”这个词稍作停顿。我是在上世纪七十年代末八十年代初开始教授这门课的，那时文学理论正值风靡一时。我的一位同事半开玩笑地说，他真希望门口能摆着黑色皮质的售货亭。理论既炙手可热又略显冷门，因此，人们对它不仅有自己的观点，而且是非常强烈的观点。结果，很多人认为理论不能被称作“导论”。他们的意思是，你不能只讲一个概览，然后说：“如果是星期二，那一定是福柯；如果是星期四，那一定是拉康。” 那样对待理论是一种背叛。人们认为，我们需要做的是彻底地去把握所有可能理论的基础。你是女权主义者、马克思主义者，还是保罗·德曼的学生？如果你要教授任何类似概论之类的课程，那么其余部分都必须从你的基本信念中推导出来。

So much then for literature and its contexts in theory. Now let me pause quickly over the word “introduction.” I started teaching this course in the late 1970s and 1980s, when literary theory was a thing absolutely of the moment. I had a colleague who was only half joking when he said he wished he had the black leather concession at the door. Theory was both hot and cool, and it was something about which, following from that, one had not just opinions but very, very strong opinions. In consequence, a lot of people thought that you couldn’t teach an “introduction” to theory. They meant that you couldn’t teach a survey, saying, “If it’s Tuesday, it must be Foucault. If it’s Thursday, it must be Lacan.” It was a betrayal to approach theory that way. What was called for, it was thought, was a radical effort to grasp the basis for all possible theory. You were a feminist or a Marxist or a student of Paul de Man, and if you were going to teach anything like a survey you had to derive the rest of it from your fundamental conviction.

那时候教理论课就是这种感觉。教入门课很尴尬。我教这门课的时候，它叫文学Y（Lit Y），是当时文学专业学生的必修课，现在也是。与此同时，保罗·德曼（Paul de Man）也在教文学Z（Lit Z），也就是他实践中的诠释艺术。那门课确实对其他所有理论形式都产生了影响，它极其严谨有趣，但它并非概览。它理所当然地认为其他一切都源于一个基本理念，但它丝毫没有想到，一系列的理念，每个理念都曾被视为基本理念，它们可以争夺关注，并以一种令人愉悦的折衷方式混合搭配——而这或许正是我们在入门课中时不时会做的事情。

That’s the way it felt to teach theory in those days. It was awkward teaching an introduction. While I was teaching this course, which was then called Lit Y and required for our literature major then as now, Paul de Man was teaching Lit Z, the art of interpretation as he practiced it. That course did indeed cast its shadow across every other form of theory, and it was extremely rigorous and interesting, but it wasn’t a survey. It took for granted that everything else would derive from a fundamental idea, but it didn’t for a minute suppose that a whole series of ideas, each considered fundamental in turn, could jostle for attention and get mixed and matched in a cheerfully eclectic way—which perhaps we will be seeming to do from time to time in our introductory course.

我怀念那一刻的清凉与炽热吗？既是，也不是。正如华兹华斯所说，“在那黎明，活着真是一种幸福”，我希望能够说服你们，对我们而言，“钻研理论”依然大有裨益。我们依然有自己的观点；我们需要有观点，更重要的是，我们需要意识到我们拥有这些观点。我们仍然需要认识到，正如文学新闻界普遍忽视的那样，我们的一切思考都源于理论原则。我们必须明白，我们的所作所为、所言所语，以及我们在论文和文章中所写的内容，都建立在理论前提之上。如果我们不去理解这些理论前提，我们就会天真地重复它们，却意识不到我们是如何运用它们，以及它们又是如何运用我们的。因此，理解理论比以往任何时候都更加重要。

Do I miss the coolness and heat of that moment? Yes and no. As Wordsworth says, “Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive,” and I hope to convince you that it’s still advantageous for us too to be “into theory.” We still have views; we need to have them and above all to recognize that we have them. We still have to recognize, as literary journalism by and large does not, that whatever we think derives from theoretical principles. We have to understand that what we do and say, what we write in our papers and articles, is grounded in theoretical premises that, if we don’t come to terms with them, we will naively reproduce without being fully aware of how we’re using them and how, indeed, they are using us. So it is as crucial as ever to understand theory.

然而，意识到理论的光环已经褪去，热潮也已过去，这本身也是一种优势。（我这里并非指方法论，方法论在今天仍然是一个亟待解决的争论焦点。）我们现在拥有了历史的视角。我们将要研究的内容，实际上很多，已不再被视为当今方法论的必要基础。我们将要研究的一切都曾有过辉煌的时期，并作为一种范式间接地影响着其他范式，但其中很多内容已不再是持续讨论的话题——这为我们提供了历史的视角。因此，我有时能够比较自信地解释为什么某些理论问题和思想会在特定的历史时期脱颖而出。有了这一额外的维度，导论的价值不仅体现在我们这些只想了解要点的人身上。它还很有价值，因为它表明，一方面，理论现在已成为一个历史话题；另一方面，它又是我们非常关注并仍然致力于研究的领域。所有这些都是开设文学理论导论课的理由。

Yet there’s an advantage too in realizing that the cachet of theory has waned and the heat of the moment has passed. (I am not speaking here of methodology, which is as much as ever a matter of urgent dispute today.) We have the vantage point of what we can now call history. Some of what we’ll be studying, indeed much of it, is no longer considered essential groundwork for today’s methodologies. Everything we’ll study has had its moment of flourishing and has remained indirectly influential as a paradigm that shapes other paradigms, but much of it is no longer lingered over as a matter for ongoing discussion—which gives us the opportunity for historical perspective. Hence from time to time I’ll be able to be reasonably confident in explaining why certain theoretical issues and ideas pushed themselves into prominence at certain historical moments. With this added dimension an introduction becomes valuable not only for those of us who simply wish to cover the high points. It’s valuable also in showing how theory is, on the one hand, now a historical topic, yet is, on the other hand, something that we’re very much engaged in and still committed to. All that then by way of rationale for teaching an introduction to the theory of literature.

文学理论与批评史有何关联？批评史也是我喜欢教授的一门课程；我通常会讲授柏拉图与T·S·艾略特、柏拉图与I·A·理查兹，或是二十世纪早期其他一些重要人物之间的联系。这门课程与文学理论有一个重要的共同点：文学批评和文学理论一样，始终关注文学的定义。我在讨论文学定义时提出的许多问题，对文学批评和文学理论都同样重要。然而，我们都本能地知道，这两者截然不同。首先，文学理论忽略了文学批评所默认的东西。文学理论并不关注评价。文学理论认为评价或欣赏是任何读者反应体验的一部分，而更倾向于探讨描述、分析和推测等问题，正如我之前所说。或者更准确地说：某些读者在特定条件下如何以及为何重视文学作品，或为何不重视或拒绝重视文学作品，这的确是文学理论，或者至少是受理论影响的方法论的研究对象；但我们为何应该或不应该重视文学作品或个别作品，则完全属于批评的范畴。不过，我必须补充一点，理论有时蕴含着价值，即便它从未声称自己拥有价值。菲利普·西德尼爵士的“诗歌不肯定任何事物，因此也从不说谎”，保罗·德曼对此深表赞同，这句话既适用于理论，也适用于批评。

How does literary theory relate to the history of criticism? The history of criticism is a course that I like to teach, too; usually I teach Plato to T. S. Eliot or Plato to I. A. Richards or some other important figure in the early twentieth century. It’s a course that shares one important feature with literary theory: literary criticism is, like theory, perpetually concerned with the definition of literature. Many of the issues that I raised in talking about defining literature are as relevant for literary criticism as they are for literary theory. Yet we all instinctively know that these are two very different enterprises. For one thing, literary theory loses something that literary criticism just takes for granted. Literary theory is not concerned with evaluation. Literary theory just takes evaluation, or appreciation, for granted as part of the responsive experience of any reader and prefers, rather, to dwell on questions of description, analysis, and speculation, as I’ve said. Or to be a little more precise: how and why certain readers under certain conditions value literature or fail or refuse to do so is indeed an object of literary theory, or at least of theory-inflected methodology, but why we should or should not value literature or individual works belongs only in the domain of criticism. I should say in qualification, though, that theory sometimes implies value even though it never lays claim to it. Sir Philip Sidney’s “poetry nothing affirmeth and therefore never lieth,” with which Paul de Man would agree completely, speaks both to theory and criticism.

这就是理论所缺失的；但理论又获得了哪些批评所缺乏的东西呢？接下来，我将回到接下来讲座将重点讨论的主题。理论的新之处在于它包含了一种怀疑主义的元素，而文学批评——通常肯定某种经典——在很大程度上并不具备这种元素。文学理论对其研究对象的基础持怀疑态度，而且在很多情况下，也对其自身论证的基础持怀疑态度。这究竟是如何产生的？为什么对诠释的真实性或肯定真理的可能性抱有怀疑会如此普遍，尤其是在二十世纪及以后？

So that’s what’s lost in theory; but what’s gained in theory that’s missing in criticism? Here I return to the topic that will occupy most of my attention for the remainder of the lecture. What’s new in theory is the element of skepticism that literary criticism—which is usually affirming a canon of some sort—does not share for the most part. Literary theory is skeptical about the foundations of its subject matter and also, in many cases, about the foundations of its own arguments. How on earth did this come about? Why should doubt about the veridical or truth-affirming possibilities of interpretation be so widespread, especially in the twentieth century and beyond?

这里我想用一点思想史来回答这个问题。我认为我所说的这种怀疑主义的种子，是在通常被称为“现代性”的时期播下的。现代性不应与现代主义混淆，后者是二十世纪初的一种现象。现代性指的是现代思想史，我们可以将其追溯到笛卡尔、莎士比亚和塞万提斯所处的“早期现代”时期。请注意这些人物的共同点：笛卡尔在他的《第一沉思录》中思考，他如何才能确定自己没有疯，或者他的思想是否被邪恶的天才所控制。莎士比亚关注的是像哈姆雷特这样可能疯也可能不疯的人物。塞万提斯笔下的主人公是一个疯子——或者至少我们几乎可以肯定这一点，但堂吉诃德显然不是。他理所当然地认为自己是一个理性而有条理的思考者。我们都认为自己是理性的，但塞万提斯让我们不禁思考，我们究竟是如何知道自己不是像堂吉诃德那样妄想妄想的呢？

Here by way of answer is a dollop of intellectual history. I think the seeds of the sort of skepticism I mean are planted during what often is called “modernity.” Modernity should not be confused with modernism, an early twentieth-century phenomenon. Modernity refers to the history of modern thought as we trace it back to the “early modern” time of Descartes, Shakespeare, and Cervantes. Notice something about all of those figures: Descartes in his First Meditation wonders how he can know for sure that he isn’t mad or whether his mind has been taken over by an evil genius. Shakespeare is preoccupied with figures like Hamlet who may or may not be crazy. Cervantes makes his hero a figure who is crazy—or at least we’re pretty sure of that, but Quixote certainly isn’t. He takes it for granted that he is a rational and systematic thinker. We all take ourselves to be rational, too, but Cervantes makes us wonder just how we know ourselves not to be paranoid delusives like Don Quixote.

所有这些关于理性思维基础的质疑都出现在十七世纪。那么，为什么我们现在会对“我所知”与“我如何知道”之间的关系感到如此不安呢？我认为，这至少部分源于笛卡尔在其《沉思录》中的论述。笛卡尔回答了他自己提出的问题：他如何才能认识到自身的存在？这个问题部分取决于他是否认定一个与他自身不同的、存在着的“异己”并不存在——他通过“我思故我在”这句话来满足自己的好奇心；此外，作为必然结果，我思故我在的一切事物也都可以被理解为存在。

All these doubts about the basis of thought in reason arise in the seventeenth century. Why then do we get this nervousness about the relationship between what I know and how I know it arising at this moment? Well, I think it’s characterized at least in part by what Descartes goes on to say in his Meditations. Descartes answers the question he has posed about how he can know himself to exist, which depends in part on deciding that an existing alien being doesn’t exist as it were in his place—he answers this question to his own satisfaction by saying, “I think. Therefore, I am”; and furthermore, as a concomitant, I think, therefore all the things that I’m thinking about can be understood to exist as well.

如今，这场“笛卡尔革命”为我们接下来150年的启蒙运动奠定了核心前提。从此，人们便认为心灵与它所思考的事物之间存在着距离。起初，这种距离被认为是极其有利的。毕竟，如果你看一幅画太近，或者离得太远，你就看不清楚——画面模糊不清——但如果你与它保持恰到好处的距离，画面就会清晰起来。科学客观性的理念，正是法国启蒙运动人物创作伟大百科全书的动力所在——而这一理念恰恰建立在维持感知者与被感知者之间这种客观的中间距离之上。然而，这种认为主体与客体之间的距离既不过大也不过小的假设逐渐开始瓦解。1796年，康德——尽管他的大多数严肃学生并不认同他属于怀疑论者阵营——却说出了与笛卡尔的“我思故我在”同样著名，甚至更加令人不安的话：“我们无法认识自在之物。”诚然，康德为自在之物构建了如此宏伟的框架——尽管我们无法认识它，但我们可以通过各种方式对其进行三角测量，并间接地理解它——因此，将他归入怀疑论者阵营似乎有些不近人情。然而，与此同时，在这种思考中，主体与客体之间的距离也开始显现出一种危险感。

Now this “Cartesian revolution” establishes a central premise for what we call the Enlightenment of the next 150 years. Thenceforth it was given that there is a distance between the mind and the things that it thinks about. At first this distance was considered highly fortunate. After all, if you look too closely at a picture or if you stand too far away from it you don’t see it clearly—it’s out of focus—but if you achieve just the right distance from it, it comes into focus. The idea of scientific objectivity, the idea that motivates the creation of the great Encyclopedia by the figures of the French Enlightenment—that idea depends on maintaining this objective middle distance between the perceiver and the perceived. Gradually, however, the supposition that this distance is neither too great nor too small begins to erode, so that in 1796 Kant, who isn’t enlisted on the side of the skeptics by most of his serious students, nevertheless does say something equally as famous as the “cogito” of Descartes and a good deal more disturbing: “We cannot know the thing in itself.” To be sure, Kant erected such a magnificent scaffolding around the thing in itself—the variety of ways in which, although we can’t know the thing, we can triangulate it and come to terms with it obliquely—that it seems churlish to enlist him on the side of the skeptics. Yet at the same time there’s a sense of danger in the distance between subject and object that begins to emerge in thinking of this kind.

到了1807年，黑格尔在《精神现象学》中指出，在近代史和意识的近期发展中，某种不幸的现象已经出现。我们拥有“不幸的意识”，一种疏离的心理状态，它使我们与所观察的对象渐行渐远。我们不再确定自己所观察的是什么，因此，意识感到疏离。在这里，我们看到主流思想史的一个发展趋势，它为怀疑主义打开了大门。但关键的转变尚未发生，因为在所有这些论述中，甚至包括黑格尔的论述，都对意识拥有思考其所思考内容的权威性毫不怀疑。意识或许对对象思考得不够清晰，但它仍然是自身思想的起源，尽管这些思想可能充满不确定性。然而，随后出现了三位伟大的思想家——当然还有其他人物，但这三位被认为是奠基人——他们开始提出一些问题，使整个意识问题变得复杂化。他们认为，意识不仅无法清晰理解它所观察的对象，因而与之疏离，而且还与其自身的根基相疏离，它既不清楚自身的来源，也不清楚它所观察的对象。换句话说，意识不仅与世界疏离，而且与其自身思想的源泉也失去了根基。

By 1807, Hegel in The Phenomenology of Mind is saying that in recent history and in recent developments of consciousness something unfortunate has set in. We have “unhappy consciousness,” an estranged state of mind that drives us too far away from the thing that we’re looking at. We are no longer certain of what we’re looking at, and consciousness, therefore, feels alienated. Here you see a development in the mainstream of intellectual history that opens the door to skepticism. But the crucial shift hasn’t yet come about, because in all of these accounts, even that of Hegel, there is still no doubt about the authority of consciousness to think what it thinks. It may not think clearly enough about objects, but it is still the origin of its own thoughts, uncertain as they may be. But then come three great figures—there are others but these are considered the foundational figures—who begin to raise questions that complicate the whole issue of consciousness. They argue not only that consciousness doesn’t clearly understand what it’s looking at and is therefore alienated from it but also that consciousness is alienated from its own underpinnings, that it doesn’t have any clear sense of where it’s coming from any more than what it’s looking at. In other words, consciousness is not only estranged from the world but deracinated from the sources of its own thoughts.

在《资本论》中关于商品拜物教的著名论证中，马克思描述了我们如何将人类劳动的产物转化为商品，并声称其具有客观价值，而非生产该商品的劳动价值。他将商品拜物教比作宗教：上帝是人类智力劳动的产物，我们将其客观化并视为自身的生产者，赋予其永恒不变的商品价值。马克思论证的一个方面是，意识，即我们相信事物的方式，是受制于自身无法控制的因素：社会、历史和经济因素塑造了我们自以为是的、真实的观念，从而产生了马克思所谓的意识形态。

Marx, in the famous argument about commodity fetishism in Das Kapital, describes the way in which we take a product of human labor and turn it into a commodity by saying that it has objective value, not the value of the labor that produced it. He compares commodity fetishism with religion: God is a product of human intellectual labor that we objectify and posit as the producer of ourselves, having the timeless, immutable value of a commodity. One aspect of Marx’s argument is that consciousness, the way in which we believe things, is deluded because it is determined by factors outside its control: social, historical, and economic factors that shape what we suppose to be our own authentic ideas, creating what Marx calls ideology.

因此，到了十九世纪中叶，意识面临的挑战是双重的：它不仅要应对自身与所观察事物之间被意识形态扭曲的虚假关系，还要应对自身与自身根基——塑造资产阶级世界观并使其看似普世的“真实存在条件”——之间虚假的关系。尼采也面临着类似的挑战，但他转换了攻击点。在尼采看来，意识运作的虚假之处在于语言本身的性质。当我们自以为在讲述真理时，实际上我们只是在使用陈旧的修辞手法。“那么，真理是什么？是一支流动的隐喻、转喻、拟人化的军队——简而言之，是人际关系的总和，这些关系在诗意和修辞上被强化……如今它们不再像货币那样具有价值，而是被贬低了。”如今，这个词非常有趣，但那些后来试图援引尼采来反驳语言真理主张的人却往往忽略了这一点。尼采似乎设想过这样一个时代：语言或许能够命名现实，语言领域的货币拥有真正的交换价值。他认为，如今语言已经沦为对陈旧比喻的征服性入侵，而所有这些比喻都左右着我们对真理的认知。我们用比喻的方式谈论天地之间的关系，很快就相信存在一位天神。我们从言语滑向信仰，不知不觉地使用着那些无法——或者说早已无法——验证的修辞手法。

So by the mid-nineteenth century the challenge to consciousness is twofold: it struggles not only with its inauthentic relationship with the things it looks at, distorted by ideology, but also with its inauthentic relationship with its own underpinnings, the “real existing conditions” that shape the bourgeois outlook and make it seem universal. The argument is a parallel one for Nietzsche, but he shifts the ground of attack. For Nietzsche, what makes the operations of consciousness inauthentic is the nature of language itself. When we think we’re telling the truth, we’re actually using worn-out figures of speech. “What then is truth? A mobile army of metaphors, metonymies, anthropomorphisms—in short, a sum of human relations which became poetically and rhetorically intensified … and are now no longer of account as coins but are debased.” That word now is very interesting and not always noticed by those who have since wished to enlist Nietzsche for polemics against truth claims in language. Nietzsche appears to imagine a time when perhaps language was capable of naming reality, when the coin of the verbal realm had real exchange value, arguing that language has now reduced itself to a conquering invasion of worn-out figures, all of which dictate what we believe to be true. We speak in a figurative way about the relationship between the earth and the sky and soon believe there’s a sky god. We slide from speech into belief, unwittingly using figures of speech that are not—or not any longer—verifiable.

弗洛伊德最终论证了意识（即我每时每刻认为自己在想什么、说什么）与决定意识的因素（在他看来是无意识）之间存在着平行关系。无意识不断地干扰着我们每时每刻的所思所言。在《日常生活心理病理学》中，弗洛伊德提醒我们，弗洛伊德式口误并非偶尔发生——这一点，即兴演讲者对此深有体会——而是时时刻刻都在发生。弗洛伊德式口误，人们隐约能将其视为意识在无意识影响下的滑落，但在弗洛伊德看来，它代表着理性对欲望的永恒且不可避免的屈从。

Freud finally argues for a parallel relationship between consciousness—what I think I am thinking and saying from minute to minute—and what determines it, in his case the unconscious, which perpetually undermines what we think and say from minute to minute. In The Psychopathology of Everyday Life, Freud reminded us that the Freudian slip isn’t something that happens just sometimes—and nobody knows this better than an ad-libbing lecturer—it’s something that happens all the time. The Freudian slip is something that one dimly recognizes as the slipping of consciousness under the influence of the unconscious, yet for Freud it represents the perpetual, inescapable subjection of reason to desire.

保罗·利科是一位诠释学传统的现代哲学家，他并不完全认同马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德的观点。在附录的第三段中，他反驳说，这些近代思想——尤其是现代文学理论——的伟大先驱共同主导了一种“怀疑学派”。怀疑（Suspicion）一词，如同怀疑主义（Skepticism）一样，也可以理解为否定。也就是说，在这种思维模式下，我们所观察的一切事物，无论其看起来多么显而易见、多么显而易见或多么显而易见，都会被一种反直觉的否定所瓦解。由于否定是辩证的，是对既定假设的逆转，它不仅会限定我们自以为确知的事物（任何人都可以认同，社会经济因素、语言和无意识会对思想产生一定的影响），而且会彻底颠覆这些事物。马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德作为强烈的否定思想家的接受方式，产生了巨大的影响。在下一讲中，我们将研读福柯的《何谓作者？》，届时我们将再次探讨马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德的思想是如何被接受的，以及鉴于福柯认为相信存在作者是危险的（因为我们很快就会将他们奉为权威），我们应该如何看待这些接受度。但如果相信存在作者是出于这个原因而危险，那么马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德——他们都是福柯本人的重要先驱——又该如何解释呢？福柯在《何谓作者？》中直面了这个问题，并给出了一个令人瞩目的答案，正如我们将看到的。对我们而言，我刚才讨论的这些段落，以及这三位作者的全部著作，其后续影响在很大程度上可以解释我们今天的主题——我们所研究的文学理论现象。换句话说，由于这些人物的影响，文学理论在很大程度上是一种怀疑的诠释学，一种否定性的实践，这一点既被其支持者所认可，也一度被其敌人强烈地否定。

Paul Ricoeur, a modern philosopher in the hermeneutic tradition who didn’t fully believe Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, retorted in the third passage in the appendix that these great precursors of recent thought—and particularly of modern literary theory—together dominate a “school of suspicion.” Suspicion, like skepticism, is a word that can also be understood as negation. That is to say, whatever seems manifest or obvious or patent in what we are looking at is undermined for this kind of mind by a negation that is counterintuitive. Because it is dialectical, the reversal of what has been posited, negation does not just qualify what we suppose ourselves to know for certain (anyone might agree by the way that socioeconomic influences, language, and the unconscious exert some influence on thought), but undermines it altogether. The reception of Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud as strong negative thinkers has been tremendously influential. When we read Foucault’s “What Is an Author?” for the next lecture, we’ll return to the question of how Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud have been received and what we should make of that in view of Foucault’s idea that it’s dangerous to believe that there are authors because we soon turn them into authorities. But if it’s dangerous to believe that there are authors for that reason, what about Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, all of them powerful precursors of Foucault himself? Foucault confronts this question in “What Is an Author?” and responds, as we’ll see, with a striking turn of thought. For us, the aftermath of the very passages I have just discussed, and certainly of the oeuvres of their three authors, can to a large degree be understood as accounting for our topic—the phenomenon of literary theory as we study it. In other words, literary theory, because of the influence of these figures, is to a considerable degree a hermeneutics of suspicion, an exercise in negation recognized as such both by its proponents and, at one time vociferously, by its enemies.

在我最初教授这门课程的那段时间，铺天盖地的抨击文学理论的文章层出不穷，其中许多面向大众读者，也有一些出自学术界人士之手。如今，文学理论可有可无，人们对此也鲜有关注；但当时人们对它的强烈反对，恰恰反映了它强大的吸引力。对许多人来说——其中大多数人似乎一度都在著书立说——文学理论与我们所知的文明的终结息息相关。对基础知识的瓦解——这似乎是文学理论诸多发展的驱动力——被视为学院派理性面临的主要威胁，并因此在无数激烈的论战中遭到猛烈抨击。我认为，此时此刻最应该强调的是，这场针对文学理论的反击，部分源于理论本身固有的怀疑主义，因为如今人文学科依然饱受争议，只是侧重点有所不同。对人文学科的攻击主要主题不再是其消极性，而是——有时是其隐含的结果——其无用性。

During the period when I was first teaching this course, a veritable six-foot shelf of diatribes against literary theory was being written, many for popular audiences, some with academic credentials. Today you can take or leave literary theory without much fuss being made about it; but the incredible outcry against it at that time reflected its dynamic appeal. For many, many people, most of whom for a while seemed to be writing books, literary theory had something to do with the end of civilization as we know it. The undermining of foundational knowledge, which seemed to motivate so much that went on in literary theory, was seen as the main threat to rationality emanating from the academy and was attacked for that reason in countless lively polemics. That the counterinsurgency against literary theory arose in part from theory’s characteristic skepticism is what I have thought it best to emphasize at the present time, because today the humanities are still under fire but with a different emphasis. The main theme of the attacks on the humanities is no longer their negativity but—sometimes as an implied result—their uselessness.

我认为，里科尔在其否定神祇体系中遗漏了一个影响深远的人物，那就是达尔文。我们可以预见，在21世纪，达尔文对文学理论和其他理论的影响将日益显著。达尔文完全可以被视为第四位持怀疑态度的诠释学家。他本人对怀疑并不感兴趣，认为自然选择对广义的宗教构不成真正的威胁，但他无疑是意识思维方式的奠基人之一，这些思维方式将意识视为一种决定论，例如社会生物学决定论、认知科学领域决定论、人工智能决定论等等。所有这些思想都源于达尔文，并将在21世纪产生越来越大的影响。我认为，真正将改变20世纪文学理论格局的，是对认知科学和社会生物学方法的日益重视，这种重视不仅体现在文学研究上，也体现在阐释过程中。而这些方法的产生，正如20世纪的某些思想脉络源于我之前讨论的三位人物一样，都源于达尔文。

I think that one influence Ricoeur leaves out of his negative pantheon, one that we can expect to become more and more important for literary theory and other kinds of theory in the twenty-first century, is that of Darwin. Darwin could very easily be considered a fourth hermeneutist of suspicion. He himself was not interested in suspicion, seeing in natural selection no real threat to religion broadly conceived, but he was certainly the founder of ways of thinking about consciousness that see it as determined, sociobiologically determined or determined in the realm of cognitive science, determined as artificial intelligence, and so on. All of this thinking descends from Darwin and will be increasingly influential in the twenty-first century. What will alter the shape of literary theory as it was known and studied in the twentieth century is, I think, an increasing emphasis on cognitive science and sociobiological approaches both to literature and to interpretive processes that will derive from Darwin in the same way that strands of thinking of the twentieth century derive from the three figures that I’ve discussed.

但怀疑的诠释学首先引发的是一种不安的气氛，这种气氛也受到历史巨变的影响；这最终让我想到亨利·詹姆斯1903年的小说《大使》和契诃夫1904年的小说《樱桃园》中的一些段落。我必须强调，这是一个特定的历史时刻。在这两部作品中，叙述者都认为意识——即活着并作为个体在世界中行动的感觉——不再包含能动性：他们感觉，某种程度上，有意识就如同一个傀儡，我们的活动范围受到了严重的限制。《大使》中的斯特雷瑟和《樱桃园》中的叶皮霍多夫所表达的观点，呼应了当时弥漫的悲观情绪，却又惊人地预示了那些更加系统化、更具启发性的文本。我想在下一讲中，先探讨詹姆斯和契诃夫的段落，然后再深入探讨“什么是作者？”这个问题。

But what the hermeneutics of suspicion gave rise to first is something like an uneasy feeling in the air, contributed to also by sweeping historical changes; and this brings me finally to a preview of the passages from Henry James’s 1903 The Ambassadors and from Chekhov’s 1904 The Cherry Orchard. I am at pains to remind you that this is a specific historical moment. In both cases the speaker argues that consciousness—the feeling of being alive and being someone acting in the world—no longer involves agency: the feeling that somehow to be conscious is merely to be a puppet, that there are severe limits to our scope of activity. Strether in The Ambassadors and Yepihodov in The Cherry Orchard speak for a point of view that echoes the doom and gloom in the air, yet strikingly anticipates texts that are much more systematically informed. I want to begin the next lecture by taking up the passages from James and Chekhov before plunging into the question “What is an author?”

 

 

第二章

CHAPTER 2

引言（续）

Introduction Continued

理论与功能化

Theory and Functionalization

阅读材料：

Readings:

福柯，米歇尔。“什么是作者？”载于《批评传统》，第 904-914 页。

Foucault, Michel. “What Is an Author?” In The Critical Tradition, pp. 904–914.

巴特，罗兰。“作者之死。”载《批评传统》，第 874-877 页。

Barthes, Roland. “The Death of the Author.” In The Critical Tradition, pp. 874–877.

摘自亨利·詹姆斯和安东·契诃夫的段落。

Passages from Henry James and Anton Chekhov.

在第一讲中，我们探讨了二十世纪文学理论为何笼罩在怀疑主义的阴影之下。但与此同时，我们也引出了另一个与怀疑主义略有不同的问题——决定论。我们指出，在思想史的进程中，首先出现的是对感知者与被感知者之间距离的担忧，这种担忧引发了对我们能否如实认知事物的怀疑。而马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德等人的思想进一步延伸出这一担忧，提出了一个更深层次的问题：我们不仅要如何如实认知事物，还要如何信任认知主体的自主性？如果意识实际上有可能——而且根据这些学者的说法，这种可能性很大——受到某种隐秘力量的支配、控制甚至“决定”，我们又如何能确定意识是独立的呢？在文学理论的论证中，决定论的重要性至少与怀疑主义不相上下。它们在很多方面显然是相互关联的，但我想在本次讲座中重点讨论决定论问题。

In the first lecture we discussed the reasons why literary theory in the twentieth century is shadowed by skepticism, but as we were talking about that we actually introduced another issue that isn’t quite the same as skepticism—namely, determinism. In the course of intellectual history, we said, first you encounter concern about the distance between the perceiver and the perceived, a concern that gives rise to skepticism about whether we can know things as they really are. But then as an outgrowth of this concern in figures like Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, you get the further question, not just how we can know things as they really are but how we can trust the autonomy of that which knows. How can we be certain that consciousness is independent if in fact there’s a chance—a good chance, according to these writers—that consciousness is in turn governed by, controlled by, “determined” by, hidden agencies? Determinism is at least as important in the arguments of literary theory as skepticism. They’re plainly interrelated in many ways, but I want to focus in this lecture on the question of determinism.

在上一讲中，我继里科尔之后，提到了马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德，认为他们是开启理论消极论调的关键人物，之后我又补充了达尔文。当我们开始思考二十世纪人类能动性所遭受的种种困境时，想到达尔文似乎就显得尤为重要。各种各样的境况都威胁着我们拥有自主权的观念，威胁着我们能够独立行动，或者至少能够带着正直感而非仅仅像傀儡一样被人牵着鼻子走。尤其是在达尔文之后，我们对基因固有模式和其他类似因素的理解，让我们开始质疑我们每个人如何才能被视为自由的个体。因此，当科学界以及人文领域的声音都对那些看似如同神雷般无法逃避的历史巨变做出回应时，能动性危机也随之加剧。

In the last lecture, following Ricoeur, I mentioned Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud as key figures who inaugurated the negative mood of theory, and then I added Darwin. It seems pertinent to think of Darwin when we begin to consider the ways in which, in the twentieth century, human agency comes under siege. Circumstances of every kind have threatened the idea that we have autonomy, that we can act independently or, at least, that we can act with a sense of integrity and not just with a sense that we are being pulled by our strings like puppets. In the aftermath of Darwin in particular, our understanding of genetic hardwiring and other such factors made us begin to wonder how we could consider ourselves, each of us, to be free agents. Thus as scientific voices in addition to voices across the humanities responded to historical cataclysms that seemed as inescapable as divine thunderbolts, the crisis of agency intensified.

在这个时代的开端，我们发现了我在上一讲中介绍的契诃夫和亨利·詹姆斯的两段文字。让我们先从契诃夫的文字开始。正如你们所知，《樱桃园》讲述的是一个庄园因社会经济状况而面临的威胁，而这种威胁最终导致了1905年的孟什维克革命。小说中的人物对这种威胁做出了各种各样的反应——包括逃避。其中一个比较有趣的反应来自一个并非真正意义上的主角的家庭仆人：家仆叶皮霍多夫，他有点像个自学者。也就是说，他以一种完全不加约束的方式，了解各种思想潮流。他充满自怜，他的言谈举止比几乎任何其他人都更能体现契诃夫阴郁的知识氛围。他说：“我是一个有教养的人。我读过各种各样的名著，但我始终无法弄清楚自己应该走哪条路，确切地说，我到底想要什么。”当我引用这段独白的部分内容时，请注意他如何不断地谈论语言，以及他自身如何受制于语言的变幻莫测。他苦苦寻觅一种“恰当的表达方式”。他对书籍略知一二，并认为自己深陷于书本知识的泥沼之中。他执着于自己所受的、并非源于自身语言的制约，尤其当他或许无意间提及《哈姆雷特》时更是如此。“我该生还是该自杀？”——或者更确切地说，“生存还是毁灭？”就这样，他将自己置于他作为角色所归属的戏剧传统之中，并以一种堕落的形式展现出，他正是源自那些英雄人物表达类似忧虑的著名感召时刻之一。

At the dawn of this epoch, we find the two passages by Anton Chekhov and Henry James that I introduced in the last lecture. Let’s begin with the Chekhov. As you know, The Cherry Orchard is about the threat to a landed estate arising from the socioeconomic conditions that soon led to the Menshevik Revolution of 1905, with the characters’ varied reactions—including avoidance—to this threat. One of the more interesting reactions comes from a family retainer who is not really a protagonist: the house servant Yepihodov, who is something of an autodidact. In a completely undisciplined way, that is, he is aware of intellectual currents. He is full of self-pity, and his speeches are more characteristic of Chekhov’s gloomy intellectual milieu than are almost anyone else’s. He says, “I’m a cultivated man. I read all kinds of remarkable books and yet I can never make out what direction I should take, what it is that I want, properly speaking.” As I quote bits of this monologue, pay attention to the way he constantly talks about language and about the way he himself is subject to the vagaries of language. He searches for a mode of “properly speaking.” He is somewhat knowledgeable about books and thinks himself caught up in the matrix of book learning. He is preoccupied with his conditioning by language that is not his own, not least when perhaps unwittingly he alludes to Hamlet. “Should I live or should I shoot myself?”—or, properly speaking, “To be or not to be?” Thus he inserts himself into the dramatic tradition to which as a character he himself belongs and shows himself to be, in a debased form, derived from one of those famous charismatic moments in which a hero expresses a comparable concern.

由此可见，这里有一个被语言陷阱所困的人物。“说句实话，暂且不谈其他事，我必须说……”他是被迫这么说的。如果语言的陈词滥调允许他拥有自己的自我，他就会变成一个自私自利的人：“我必须说，就我个人而言，命运对待我无情，就像暴风雨对待一艘小船一样。” ¹文章结尾写道：“你读过巴克尔的书吗？”亨利·托马斯·巴克尔如今已鲜为人知，但他曾经的名气几乎与《西方的没落》的作者奥斯瓦尔德·斯宾格勒不相上下。巴克尔是一位维多利亚时代的历史学家，他关注西方文明的瓦解，是十九世纪末“一切都在走向毁灭”这种观念的代表人物。因此，在某种意义上，巴克尔的书正是决定叶皮霍多夫性格的文本之一。 “你读过巴克尔吗？我想和你谈谈，阿芙多佳·费奥多罗夫娜。” 这些对话中充斥着关于文字、语言、说话和书籍的词汇，这正是这个人物的困境所在。他受制于书籍和语言，尽管博览群书是他的骄傲，但他却隐约意识到这正是他的问题所在。

Here then is a character who is caught up in the snare of language. “Properly speaking and letting other subjects alone, I must say …” He is forced to say, that is. He would be an egoist if the commonplaces of language would only let him have an ego of his own: “I must say, regarding myself among other things, that fate treats me mercilessly as a storm treats a small boat.”1 And the end of the passage: “Have you read Buckle?” Henry Thomas Buckle is a forgotten name today, but at one time he was just about as famous as Oswald Spengler, who wrote The Decline of the West. Buckle was a Victorian historian preoccupied with the dissolution of Western civilization, an avatar of the notion in the late nineteenth century that everything was going to hell in a handbasket. One of the texts, then, that in a certain sense determines Yepihodov is Buckle. “Have you read Buckle? I wish to have a word with you, Avdotya Fyodorovna.” The saturation of these speeches with words about words, language, speaking, and books is just the dilemma of this character. He is book- and language-determined, and he’s obscurely aware that this is his problem even though knowing books is a source of pride for him.

那么，让我们来看一段与詹姆斯《大使》截然不同的文字。一位魅力十足的中年男子兰伯特·斯特雷瑟前往巴黎，接回朋友的儿子查德·纽瑟姆。查德将接管家族企业，这家企业在马萨诸塞州伍利特生产一种不知名的日用品——很可能是卫生纸。在巴黎，斯特雷瑟领略到了都市文化的魅力。他意识到自己错过了什么。他参加了一位雕塑家举办的派对，在那里遇到了一个名叫小比尔汉姆的年轻人。他把比尔汉姆拉到一边，滔滔不绝地说道：“别重蹈我的覆辙。别错过人生。尽情享受生活。不这样做是错误的。” 他接着说，这就是原因：

Let us turn, then, to a passage in a very different tone from James’s The Ambassadors. An altogether charming character, the late middle-aged Lambert Strether, has gone to Paris to bring home the son of a friend, Chad Newsome, who is to take over the family business, manufacturing an unnamed household article in Woollett, Massachusetts—probably toilet paper. In Paris Strether has awakened to the sheer wonder of urbane culture. He sees that he’s missed something. He goes to a party given by a sculptor, and at this party he meets a young man named Little Bilham, whom he takes aside and addresses in a long speech, saying: “Don’t do what I have done. Don’t miss out on life. Live all you can. It is a mistake not to.” And this is why, he goes on to say:

这件事——我是指人生这件事——对我来说，无疑不可能有所不同；因为它充其量就像一个锡模，要么是带凹槽和浮雕的，装饰华丽，要么是光滑而乏味的，人的意识就像一团无助的果冻，被倒入其中——正如那位伟大的厨师所说，人“接受”了它的形态，或多或少地被它牢牢地束缚：人只能尽力而为。然而，人仍然拥有自由的幻觉。
The affair—I mean the affair of life—couldn’t, no doubt, have been different for me; for it’s at the best a tin mould, either fluted and embossed, with ornamental excrescences, or else smooth and dreadfully plain, into which, a helpless jelly, one’s consciousness is poured—so that one “takes” the form as the great cook says, and is more or less compactly held by it: one lives in fine as one can. Still, one has the illusion of freedom.2

这时，比叶皮霍多夫聪明得多的斯特雷瑟说了一句非常精辟的话，我认为我们可以加以利用。他接着说：“因此，不要像我一样，忘记了那段幻觉。我当时要么太蠢，要么太聪明，以至于没有意识到它的存在。我也不知道是哪种情况。” 如果他蠢到没有意识到，那么他当然会被解放出来，进入行动的领域。他会成为尼采在一本关于历史用途的书中所说的“历史人”。他会像拥有自由一样投入生活，即使他蠢到无法认识到这种自由只是一种幻觉。另一方面，如果他聪明到无法——或者说——埋葬这种幻觉，无法像自由人一样生活，如果他聪明到做不到这一点，那么他就会成为文学理论家的原型。他就是那种始终无法忘记自由不过是一种幻觉的人，他无法摆脱二十世纪某种思维方式所特有的、令人窒息的执念。而他最后那句谨慎得令人拍案叫绝的话语——因为一个确定的存在又怎能知晓任何事呢？——“我不太清楚是哪一个。”

At this point, Strether, who is infinitely smarter than Yepihodov, says something very clever that I think we can make use of. He goes on to say, “Therefore, don’t be, like me, without the memory of that illusion. I was either at the right time too stupid or too intelligent to have it. I don’t quite know which.” Now if he was too stupid to have it, then of course he would have been liberated into the realm of action. He would have been what Nietzsche in a book about the uses of history calls “historical man.” He simply would have plunged into life as though he had freedom, even though he would have been too stupid to recognize that his freedom was an illusion. On the other hand, if he was too intelligent to—as it were—bury this illusion and live as though he were free, if he was too intelligent to do that, he would be a prototype for the literary theorist. He would be the sort of person who can’t forget long enough that freedom is an illusion to get away from the crippling preoccupations that characterize a certain kind of thinking in the twentieth century. And it’s delightfully circumspect of him that he says at last—because how can a determinate being know anything?—“I don’t quite know which.”

因此，这些典型的段落可以引出本次讲座的主题，即权威的丧失：罗兰·巴特标题中的“作者之死”，以及福柯提出的问题“什么是作者？”所蕴含的意义。随着人类主体性的否定，文学理论的第一个牺牲品就是作者，或者说是作者的概念。

So these are characteristic passages that can introduce us to this lecture’s subject, which is the loss of authority: “the death of the author” in Roland Barthes’s title and what is implied in Foucault’s question, “What is an author?” With the denial of human agency, the first sacrifice for literary theory is the author, the idea of the author.

现在让我来描述一下场景。就像斯特雷瑟的故事，但时间设定在七十年后的巴黎。地点不一定是巴黎，也可能是伯克利、哥伦比亚，甚至柏林。时间是1968年或1969年，并延续到70年代。学生和他们的大多数教授都走上街头，抗议的不仅是越南战争，还有60年代那种专制政权对示威活动的压制。一场知识分子反抗运动在巴黎以各种形式爆发，但其核心理念却迅速成为一句响亮的口号：“质疑权威”。因此，法国最杰出的知识分子在学生运动的高潮时期写下了一篇题为《何谓作者？》的文章。

Now let me set the scene. Like Strether but seventy years later, we’re in Paris. It wouldn’t have to be Paris. It could be Berkeley or Columbia or maybe Berlin. It’s 1968 or 1969, spilling over into the 1970s. Students and most of their professors are on the barricades, in protest not only against the war in Vietnam but also against the authoritarian resistance to protest that marked the 1960s. A ferment of intellectual revolt takes all sorts of forms in Paris but is largely organized by what quickly became a bumper sticker in this country: “Question authority.” Hence the most prominent intellectual in France writes an essay at the very peak of the student uprising entitled “What Is an Author?”

然而，福柯对这个问题给出了一系列带有历史色彩的答案，这些答案绝非直白或简单。或许你已经预料到我刚才提到的历史背景和福柯的作用，因此对他的实际论述感到比预期的更加困惑和沮丧。但你也看到了，《何谓作者？》一书的批判精神与你的预期完全一致。由于这是一门入门课程，我不会过多地探讨福柯论证中那些出人意料的转折；相反，我会着重强调你可能已经预料到的部分。

Yet Foucault offers a series of historically inflected answers to this question that are by no means straightforward or simple. Maybe you anticipated what I’ve just been saying about the historical setting and about the role of Foucault and were therefore more confused and frustrated by what he actually says than you expected to be. Yet you also saw that “What Is an Author?” nonetheless is written as much in the spirit of critique as you had anticipated. Because this course is introductory, I won’t spend a great deal of time with the more unexpected turns of Foucault’s argument; I’ll emphasize, rather, the parts you may have anticipated.

现在，我们大多数人可能会皱起眉头，质疑福柯本人是否真的不认为自己是作者。毕竟，他可是个超级巨星，习惯了被人认真对待。他是不是想说，他并非权威，而只是“作者功能”？他文章的文本领域是一系列结构操作，人们可以从中发现作者，就像发现情节或语法要素一样？嗯，这有点像皇帝的新衣，我们最终还是要认真对待这个问题。但我们可以采取一些方法来避免直接面对它，甚至消除它的威胁，而这些方法值得我们去探索。

Now most of us are likely to raise our eyebrows and ask whether this Foucault person really doesn’t think he himself is an author. After all, he’s a superstar. He’s used to being taken very seriously. Does he want to say that he’s not an authority but just an “author function,” that the textual field of his own essay is a set of structural operations within which one can discover, just as one discovers a plot or an element of grammar, an author? Well, this is an emperor’s new clothes sort of question that we’re going to take seriously in the long run, but there are ways of keeping the question at arm’s length, even of disarming it, and they need to be explored.

所以，没错，这位听起来很有权威的人似乎是一位作家。我从未见过比福柯更像作家的人，然而他却在质疑是否存在作家这种东西，或者说，如果存在，那么确定作家究竟是什么又有多难。让我先讲个轶事，或许有助于我们理解这位明星作家与“作家不存在”的思想氛围之间这种奇特的联系。我的一位前同事在20世纪60年代在约翰·霍普金斯大学选修了一门课程。授课老师是乔治·普莱，一位“现象学批评家”，很遗憾我们这次的综述没能抽出时间来介绍他的重要著作。无论如何，他是一位明星作家。普莱滔滔不绝地讲着课，学生们时不时会举手说出一个名字。有个学生举手说：“马拉美。”普莱会说：“没错！绝对没错！”然后继续讲课。然后，另一个人会举手说：“普鲁斯特。”“啊，准确！普鲁斯特。普鲁斯特。”然后又回到讲台上。于是我的同事决定凭直觉行事。他举手说：“伏尔泰”，一位著名作家，但理论家们通常不会对他感兴趣。果然，普莱一脸困惑地说：“什么？……我不明白。”然后带着茫然的神情继续讲课。

So yes, this very authoritative-sounding person would seem to be an author. I never met anybody who seemed more like an author than Foucault, yet he’s asking whether there is any such thing as one, or in any case how difficult it is to decide what it is if there is. Let me digress with an anecdote that may help us to understand this odd connection between a star author and the atmosphere of thought in which there is no such thing as an author. A former colleague of mine was taking a lecture course at Johns Hopkins in the 1960s. The course was given by Georges Poulet, a “phenomenological critic” whose important work I regret not having time to cover in our survey. He was, in any case, a star author. Poulet would be lecturing away, and the students from time to time would raise their hand and simply utter a name. One would raise her hand and say, “Mallarmé.” And Poulet would say, “Mais oui! Exactement!” and then go on with his lecture. Then somebody else would raise his hand and say, “Proust.” “Ah, précisement! Proust. Proust.” Then back to the lecture. So my colleague decided to act on a hunch. He raised his hand and said, “Voltaire,” a famous author but not one in whom theorists typically find anything of interest. Sure enough, Poulet looked puzzled and said “Quoi donc?… Je ne vous comprends pas,” then returned in a state of bemusement to his lecture.

如今，这种提及人名的惯例实际上表明，它们不仅仅是名字，甚至不仅仅是明星的名字。它们显然代表着某种超越单纯作者身份的东西，代表着有趣的“话语”领域或范畴。普莱特是一位理论家，他认为一位作家的全部作品是一个整体，可以被理解为一个结构整体，而他的评论也正是朝着这个方向努力的。他会谈到“马拉美恩的文本”或“普鲁斯特的文本”。在这种语境下，提及一位作家就等于指明了一个领域。当然，我的同事——因为他非常清楚，当他提到“伏尔泰”时，普莱特肯定不会理会——也领悟到了这一点。话语领域既有相关的、有趣的，也有完全无关的。我们或许会自发地做出这些区分，但我们需要意识到，当我们赋予这些领域作者身份时，我们很可能想到的不是某种有意的意识，而是孤立的文本效果，是许多其他文本特征中的“签名”，这些特征不一定是作者的痕迹，而是——例如——超个人的语言效果或场合的限制。

Now this ritual of dropping names actually shows that they are not just names, not even just the names of stars. They are plainly names that stand for something other than mere authorship, names that stand for domains or fields of interesting “discourse.” Poulet was the kind of theorist who believed that the oeuvre of an author was a totality that could be understood as a structural whole, and his commentaries worked toward that end. He would speak of “le texte mallarméen” or “le texte proustien.” In this context, to refer to an author is to name a domain. That’s of course what my colleague—because he knew perfectly well that when he said “Voltaire,” Poulet would have nothing to do with it—had figured out. There were relevant and interesting fields of discourse and there were completely irrelevant fields of discourse. We spontaneously make these distinctions, perhaps, but we need to be aware that when we accord authorship to such fields we may well be thinking not of some intending consciousness but of isolated textual effects, “signatures” amid many other textual features that are not necessarily authorial traces but—for example—transpersonal language effects or the constraints of an occasion.

在普莱和福柯的时代，理论家们喜欢谈论“话语”或“话语性”，而不是作者的言语。我上次说过，有时人们在试图定义文学时会束手无策，干脆说文学就是任何人说的任何东西。这些人更倾向于使用“话语”、“文本场域”或“话语性”这样的词，而不是“文学”。就像许多术语一样，这种迂回的说法也有其道理。“话语”或“话语性”被理解为话语成为讨论场域的潜力，这表明作者之间以及不同类型的言语之间的界限极其模糊。人们可以谨慎地谈论文学话语、政治话语、人类学话语，但却不愿直接说文学、政治学、人类学；同样，“范妮·伯尼”、“玛丽亚·埃奇沃思”、“简·奥斯汀”、“乔治·普莱”、“米歇尔·福柯”和“茨维坦·托多罗夫”这些名字并非封闭的领地，而是开放的领域。这些话语习惯源于对各种话语形式彼此渗透性的感知；而这种习惯挑战了某些话语形式可以被理解为合法私有财产的观念。

Theorists in Poulet’s and Foucault’s time liked to speak of “discourse” or “discursivity,” as opposed to authorial speech. I said last time that sometimes people just throw up their hands when they try to define literature and say that literature is whatever anyone says it is. Such people are more likely to use the word “discourse” or “textual field” or “discursivity” than the word “literature.” Like much jargon, such circumlocution does have a rationale. The word “discourse,” or “discursivity” understood as the potential of discourse to become an arena for discussion, suggests that the boundary is extremely porous both between authors and between types of speech. One can speak hesitantly of literary discourse, political discourse, anthropological discourse, but one doesn’t want to go so far as to say literature, political science, anthropology; and by the same token, the names “Fanny Burney,” “Maria Edgeworth,” and “Jane Austen,” “Georges Poulet,” “Michel Foucault,” and “Tzvetan Todorov” are open fields, not enclosed fiefdoms. These are habits of speech that arise from sensing the permeability of all forms of utterance with respect to each other; and such habits challenge the notion that certain forms of utterance can be understood as authorized pieces of private property.

最好澄清一个常见的、有时甚至是故意的误解：没有人，当然福柯，说过，也永远不会说一份书面文件没有作者，不是由某人或某些人撰写的。没错，巴特谈到了作者的“死亡”，但即便巴特也并非认为作者不存在。我们面临的问题仅仅是：在判断某个话语领域的本质时，我们是否真的必须诉诸作者的权威？我们完全可以在文本体验中找到作者，而且这样做的好处是，我们阅读的是文本本身，而不是来自上级的法令。作者是一系列实践，一种虚拟的存在，而非实际的存在：福柯称之为“功能”。现在重要的问题是：首先，我们如何识别作者的存在；其次，在试图确定文本的意义时——这将在下一讲中讨论——我们是否应该诉诸作者的权威。如果作者是一种功能，那么这种功能就是在文本的各个角落出现，或许会造成一些问题，我们需要将其与说话者或叙述者区分开来（这是你从高中英语课起就熟悉的一种思维方式），或者，在戏剧的情况下，更明显地，与角色区分开来。

Best to clear up a common, sometimes willful misunderstanding: no one, certainly not Foucault, has said or ever will say that a written document doesn’t have an author, isn’t written by some person or persons. Yes, Barthes talks about the “death” of the author, but even Barthes doesn’t mean that the author doesn’t exist. We are asked only whether we really do necessarily appeal to the authority of an author in making up our mind about the nature of a given field of discourse. We can as readily find the author somewhere within the textual experience, with the advantage that it is then a text we are reading and not a decree from above. The author is a set of practices, a virtual presence, not an actual one: what Foucault calls a “function.” The important questions now are how we recognize the author’s presence, first, and, second, whether in attempting to determine the meaning of a text—and this is something we’ll be talking about in the next lecture—we should appeal to the authority of the author. If the author is a function, that function is something that appears, perhaps problematically appears, here and there across the field of the text, something that for one thing (and this is a turn of thought you’ve been familiar with since high school English) we need to distinguish from the speaker or the narrator, or, yet more obviously in the case of plays, from the characters.

在福柯看来，文本是由互动功能构成的实体。巴特也认为文本是一个功能系统，但他更强调该系统与其他系统的可渗透性。巴特在《作者之死》（874）的开篇引用了巴尔扎克的一篇名为《萨拉辛》的短篇小说：

For Foucault a text is an entity composed of interactive functions. For Barthes, too, a text is a system of functions, but he lays more emphasis on the permeability of this system to other systems. Barthes opens “The Death of the Author” (874) by quoting a short story by Balzac called “Sarrasine”:

在巴尔扎克的小说《萨拉西娜》中，他描写一个伪装成女人的阉伶时写道：“这就是女人本身，她有突如其来的恐惧，她有非理性的奇思妙想，她有本能的担忧，她有冲动的胆大妄为，她有娇嗔的脾气，还有她那令人陶醉的敏感。 ” 是谁在说这句话？是故事的主人公，他一心想对隐藏在女人面具下的阉伶一无所知吗？是巴尔扎克本人，他从个人经历中汲取了关于女性的哲学思想吗？是作为作家的巴尔扎克，他在阐述关于女性的“文学”观点吗？是普世智慧吗？是浪漫主义心理学吗？我们永远不得而知，因为写作本身就是对一切声音、一切起源的毁灭。写作是一个中立的、复合的、斜向的空间，我们的主体（这是一个故意的双关语）滑落到否定中（“我们的主体”意味着我们有时不太清楚在谈论什么，但更重要的是，主体，作者的主体，给定说话主体的实际身份，正在滑落）在那里失去所有身份，首先是写作主体本身的身份。
In his story “Sarrasine” Balzac, describing a castrato disguised as a woman, writes the following sentence: “This was woman herself, with her sudden fears, her irrational whims, her instinctive worries, her impetuous boldness, her fussings and her delicious sensibility.” Who is speaking thus? Is it the hero of the story bent on remaining ignorant of the castrato hidden beneath the woman? Is it Balzac the individual, furnished by his personal experience with a philosophy of Woman? Is it Balzac the author professing “literary” ideas on femininity? Is it universal wisdom? Romantic psychology? We shall never know, for the good reason that writing is the destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing is that neutral, composite, oblique space where our subject [and this is a deliberate pun] slips away [“our subject” meaning that we don’t quite know what’s being talked about sometimes, but also, and more importantly, the subject, the authorial subject, the actual identity of the given speaking subject, is what slips away] into the negative where all identity is lost, starting with the very identity of the body writing.

在巴特撰写这篇文章时，他正在创作一本名为《S/Z》的专著，探讨“萨拉辛”这一主题。在这本书中，此前以“结构主义”领军人物著称的巴特，越来越关注那些看似结构性事物背后迷宫般的无形本质。尽管福柯和巴特都在同样的反权威氛围下挑战着同一权威，但巴特笔下的作者形象却比福柯更加彻底地被掩盖——对福柯而言，“消失”一词或许有些夸张。

At the time he wrote this essay, Barthes was writing a whole book about “Sarrasine” called S/Z. In this book, Barthes, known until then as a leading “structuralist,” became increasingly preoccupied with the mazelike shapelessness of what seems to be structural. Although both Foucault and Barthes are dethroning the same authority in the same antiauthoritarian climate, the author is eclipsed here more completely than in Foucault, for whom “disappear” would be an overstatement.

我认为福柯默认文本场域比巴特所设想的更具系统性，他指出，当我们谈论作者功能而非作者本身时，我们就不再提出某些问题，例如以下问题（913）：“一个自由的主体如何才能深入事物的本质并赋予其意义？它如何才能从内部激活语言的规则，从而产生真正属于它自身的设计？”换句话说，我们不再追问作者如何就其所表达的主题行使自主意志。我们不再假定意义与作者的意义一致。福柯继续说道：

Foucault, who I think does take for granted that a textual field is more firmly systematic than Barthes had come to suppose, says that when we speak of the author function rather than the author, we no longer raise certain questions, such as the following (913): “How can a free subject penetrate the substance of things and give it meaning? How can it activate the rules of a language from within and thus give rise to the designs which are properly its own?” In other words, we no longer ask how the author exerts autonomous will with respect to the subject matter being expressed. We do not suppose the meaning to coincide with the meaning of the author. Foucault continues:

相反，我们将提出以下问题：“在何种条件下，主体以何种形式出现在话语秩序中？它在每种话语类型中占据何种位置，承担何种功能，又遵循何种规则？”简而言之，[当我们以这种方式谈论作者功能时]，实际上是剥夺了主体（或其替代物）[例如，一个角色，或者一个说话者，就像我们在《我的最后一位公爵夫人》中说说话者并非作者一样]……作为发起者的角色，并将主体分析为话语中一个可变且复杂的功能。
Instead, these questions will be raised: “How, under what conditions, and in what forms can something like a subject appear in the order of discourse? What place can it occupy in each type of discourse, what functions can it assume, and by obeying what rules?” In short, [when we speak in this way of an author function] it is a matter of depriving the subject (or its substitute) [a character, for example, or a speaker, as when we say the speaker is not the author in “My Last Duchess”] … of its role as originator, and of analyzing the subject as a variable and complex function of discourse.

（此类“话语”中的“主体”始终指的是说话者的主观感受，而不是话语内容本身。）

(“The subject” in “discourse” of this kind always means the subjectivity of the speaker, not the subject matter.)

既然我们已经讨论了这么多关于福柯和巴特在“推翻作者”问题上究竟意味着什么以及不意味着什么，或许是时候为作者辩护一番了。我将代表所有想要站出来捍卫作者的人，引用塞缪尔·约翰逊在《莎士比亚序言》中的一段精彩论述。在这段话中，他解释了我们为何一直以来都对作者的权威表示敬意。这不仅仅是一个问题——正如福柯和巴特总是暗示的那样——即对权威的顺从，仿佛权威是手持警棍的警察。我们也可以将作者身份理解为人类的成就。约翰逊是这样说的：

With this much said about what Foucault and Barthes do and do not mean in dethroning the author, it’s probably time to say something in defense of the author. I will speak for all of you who want to stand up and defend the author by quoting a wonderful passage from Samuel Johnson’s “Preface to Shakespeare,” in which he explains why we have always paid homage to the authority of the author. It’s not just a question—as obviously Foucault and Barthes are always suggesting—of deferring to authority as though the authority were the police laying about them with truncheons. We can also think of authorship as human accomplishment. This is what Johnson says:

人类的成就总是与人类的能力有着无声的关联，而探究人类的构想能达到何种程度，或者人类能将自身的天赋发挥到何种高度，远比评判某项具体成就的优劣更为重要。因此，人们总是热衷于探寻创造的工具，同时也关注其精湛的工艺，以了解其中有多少归功于人类的原始能力，又有多少归功于偶然的、外在的帮助。3
There is always a silent reference of human works to human abilities, and as the inquiry, how far man may extend his designs or how high he may rate his native force, is of far greater dignity than in what rank we shall place any particular performance, curiosity is always busy to discover the instruments as well as to survey the workmanship, to know how much is to be ascribed to original powers and how much to casual and adventitious help.3

将文本领域视为一个系统固然很好，但与此同时，我们也想提醒自己自身的价值。我们想说，“作品”（某人的作品）不仅仅是一系列函数——或者说，不仅仅是实验室里的变量。它是天才的结晶。它让我们得以评价人类的能力“卓越”。尤其是在这充满苦难的时代——约翰逊对此深有体会——我们更应该如此。即便只能抓住一丝希望，我们诉诸作者的权威，并非出于畏缩的恐惧，而是出于敬意。

It’s all very well to consider a textual field as a system, but at the same time we want to remind ourselves of our worth. We want to say that a “work” (somebody’s work) is not just a set of functions—variables, as one might say in the lab. It’s produced by genius. It’s something that allows us to rate human ability “high.” Especially in this vale of tears—and Johnson is very conscious of this being a vale of tears—that’s what we want to keep doing. Clutching at such straws as we can, it is in the spirit of homage rather than in cringing fear that we appeal to the authority of an author.

但我们谈论的是不同的时代，苦难之谷的性质或许已经改变。现在是1969年，巴特和福柯都认为，诉诸作者作为父权式的权威，其目的在于规范文本的解读方式，即便是在学院内部也是如此。（索邦大学一位非常愤怒的学者曾写过一本名为《新批判，新骗局》的书来抨击巴特。）换句话说，他们都坚持认为，诉诸作者——而非将作者置于文本领域的功能性之中——是对意义可能性的一种限制或规范。

But we are speaking of different times, the vale of tears having perhaps changed in character. This is 1969, and the purpose that’s alleged for appealing to the author as a paternal source, as an authority, is, according to both Barthes and Foucault, to police the way texts are read even within the academy. (A very angry don at the Sorbonne had written a book against Barthes called Nouvelle critique, nouvelle imposture.) In other words, both of them insist that the appeal to the author—as opposed to the submersion of the author in the functionality of the textual field—is a kind of delimitation or policing of the possibilities of meaning.

让我引用两段话来佐证这一点，首先是罗兰·巴特（Roland Barthes）的观点（877）。巴特说：“一旦作者被移除，解读文本的企图就变得毫无意义。”顺便一提，巴特和福柯的观点在这里再次出现了分歧。福柯不会用“毫无意义”这个词。他会说我们可以解读文本，但作者的功能只是解读过程的一个方面。而巴特当时正处于他学术生涯的又一个阶段，在这个阶段，他认为文本结构过于复杂，以至于不再是结构本身。这与解构主义的影响密切相关，我们将在本书后面部分详细讨论。

Let me just cite two passages to that effect, first going back to Roland Barthes (877). Barthes says, “Once the Author is removed, the claim to decipher a text becomes quite futile.” By the way, once again there’s a rift here between Barthes and Foucault. Foucault wouldn’t say “quite futile.” He would say we can decipher it, but that the author function is just one aspect of the deciphering process. But Barthes had entered a phase of his career, again, in which structures seemed so complex that they ceased to be structures. This has a great deal to do with the influence of deconstruction, to which we’ll return later in the book.

总之，巴特斯继续说道：

In any case, Barthes continues:

赋予文本一个作者，就等于给文本设限，赋予其一个最终的指称，从而结束写作。这种观念非常契合批评（这里的批评很像警察——“批评”意味着做一个刻薄的批评家，进行批评），批评家因此承担起一项重要的任务：在作品之下发现作者（或其化身：社会、历史、心理、自由[即能动性]）：一旦找到了作者，文本就得到了“解释”——这是批评家的胜利。
To give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception suits criticism [criticism here is a lot like policing—“criticism” means being a nasty critic, criticizing] very well, the latter then allotting itself the important task of discovering the Author (or its hypostases: society, history, psyche, liberty [i.e., agency]) beneath the work: when the Author has been found, the text is “explained”—a victory to the critic.

换句话说，对意义的管控已经完成，批评家取得了胜利，正如20世纪60年代末的骚乱中警察获胜一样。我们可以用福柯的论断（913）来强化这种观点：“因此，作者是意识形态的象征，我们通过他来标记我们恐惧意义扩散的方式。”

In other words, the policing of meaning has been accomplished and the critic wins, just as in the uprisings of the late 1960s the cops win. We can reinforce this attitude with the pronouncement by Foucault (913): “The author is therefore the ideological figure by which one marks the manner in which we fear the proliferation of meaning.”

现在，我们很可能又要以怀疑来反驳怀疑了。你或许会说：“我为什么不应该害怕意义的泛滥？我只想知道某件事究竟意味着什么。我不想知道它有无数种含义。我来这里是为了学习事物究竟意味着什么。我不想被告知我可以在这里坐一辈子，仅仅为了分析一句话。别跟我提巴尔扎克短篇小说里那些令人头晕目眩的句子。我来这里是为了知道事物的意义。我不在乎这是否是在进行某种形式的审查。不管是什么，让我们把它完成吧。”如果你以这种不耐烦的方式回应，我能理解你的感受，因为在某种程度上，对诉诸作者这一做法被意识形态滥用的关注，很大程度上源于其特定的历史时期。在那个时代，人们几乎一提到“作者”这个词，就会想到“权威”，而一提到“权威”，就一定会想到警察。我知道——那时我还是伯克利的学生。这种思维模式或许至今仍然影响着我们许多人的生活，而且一直以来都影响着许多地方许多人的生活，我们不能忘记这一点。但是，在当今的学术界，这种观点已不再像巴特和福柯撰写这些文章时那样根深蒂固。

Now once again, we are likely to counter skepticism with skepticism. You may well say, “Why shouldn’t I fear the proliferation of meaning? I want to know what something definitely means. I don’t want to know that it means a million things. I’m here to learn what things mean in so many words. I don’t want to be told that I could sit here for the rest of my life just parsing one sentence. Don’t tell me about these vertiginous sentences from Balzac’s short story. I’m here to know what things mean. I don’t care if it’s policing or not. Whatever it is, let’s get it done.” The reason I could feel sympathy if you were to respond in this grumpy way is that to a certain extent the preoccupation with the ideological misuse of the appeal to an author belongs very much to its historical moment, a time when you could scarcely say the word “author” without thinking “authority,” and you could certainly never say the word “authority” without thinking about the police. I know—I was then a student at Berkeley.
