This is a structure of thought that perhaps pervades the lives of many of us even to this day and has always pervaded the lives of many people in many places, we mustn’t forget that, but it is not quite as much the default point of view in the academic world today as it was in the moment of these essays by Barthes and Foucault.

说了这么多，理论家该如何为某些名字（比如她自己的名字）重新赢得尊重呢？“你不是作家，但我才是”：假设有人卑鄙到怀有这种想法，你能提出一个论证，让这种想法听起来似乎有道理吗？毕竟，福柯——撇开他自己不谈，他从未提及自己——非常欣赏某些作家。特别是，他像他那一代以及其他几代人一样，欣赏马克思和弗洛伊德。如果我们对马克思和弗洛伊德没有这种感觉，就去否定作家们普遍存在的权威性——尽管我们或许可以公正地发现某些作家身上存在专制倾向——这是很危险的。福柯该如何论证，才能让那些享有特权的作家——也就是说，那些被积极引用且不会让人感到受到约束的人物——保有应有的尊重地位呢？

With all this said, how can the theorist recuperate honor for certain names like, for example, her own? “You’re not an author, but I am”: let’s suppose someone were dastardly enough to harbor such a thought. Could you develop an argument in which the thought might actually seem to make sense? After all, Foucault—setting himself aside, he doesn’t mention himself—Foucault very much admires certain writers. In particular, he admires, like so many of his generation and other generations, Marx and Freud. It’s perilous to reject the police-like authority of authors in general—in some of whom we may justly discover authoritarian tendencies—when we don’t feel that way about Marx and Freud. How can Foucault mount an argument in which privileged authors—that is to say, figures whom one cites positively and without a sense of being policed—can retain a place of honor?

顺便一提，福柯在这里没有提到尼采，但他完全可以提到，因为尼采的“谱系学”思想或许是福柯作品中最重要的影响因素。坦白说，我认为他没提到尼采纯属偶然。这对我们来说本该是一个完美的对称，因为在上一讲中我们引用了保罗·利科的话，大意是马克思、尼采和弗洛伊德这几位作者——这是利科的原话——是“大师”。哇！大师？这可是福柯最不想听到的词。那么，他是如何回避这个问题的呢？他创造了一个概念。他说，马克思和弗洛伊德不是作者，而是“话语性的奠基人”。话语性的奠基人是指那些其话语能够随着时间的推移，促成人们对话语进行建设性和进步性回应的人。在这里，他巧妙地区分了知识遗产的奠基人和在文体发展中具有影响力的创新者。他谈到安妮·拉德克利夫（他本应谈论的是霍勒斯·沃波尔，不过暂且不谈），认为她确立了一些修辞手法、主题和前提，这些手法、主题和前提在接下来的一百年里，乃至直至今日，都影响着哥特小说的写作，然而，他却认为她不应被称为话语性的奠基人。他声称，她并没有建立起一种话语体系或辩论领域，在这个领域内，思想即便不一定能被归因，也能得以发展。在我看来，这似乎相当反文学，仿佛探讨文学影响并非在于追随一位“话语性奠基人”的脚步，但我不会在此赘述。

Foucault, by the way, doesn’t mention Nietzsche here, but he might very well have done because Nietzsche’s idea of “genealogy” is perhaps the most important influence on Foucault’s work. Frankly, I think it’s just an accident that he doesn’t mention him. It would have been a perfect symmetry for us, because in the last lecture we quoted Paul Ricoeur to the effect that these authors, Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, were—and this is Ricoeur’s word—“masters.” Whoa! Masters? That’s the last word Foucault would want to hear. How, then, does he circumvent this problem? He invents a concept. He says that Marx and Freud aren’t authors but “founders of discursivity.” A founder of discursivity is someone whose discourse enables constructive and progressive responses to it over time. Here he makes a subtle distinction between founders of an intellectual legacy and influential innovators in the development of genres. He speaks of Anne Radcliffe (he should be speaking of Horace Walpole, but never mind) as a person who established certain tropes, topoi, and premises that govern the writing of gothic fiction for the next hundred years and, indeed, even up to the present, yet should not be called a founder of discursivity. She doesn’t establish a discourse or sphere of debate, he claims, within which ideas, without being attributable necessarily, can nevertheless be developed. This seems to me rather anti-literary, as though negotiating literary influence were not precisely a matter of speaking or writing in the wake of a “founder of discursivity,” but I won’t belabor the point.

福柯还致力于区分马克思和弗洛伊德这样的人物与伽利略和牛顿这样的科学家。为了支持福柯的观点，请注意，我们用“马克思主义者”或“弗洛伊德主义者”来指代人，却不会用“拉德克利夫主义者”、“伽利略主义者”或“牛顿主义者”来指代人。我们使用“牛顿主义者”这个形容词的方式，与作者无关，就像普莱特在我的轶事中使用这些词语一样，但我们不会把那些仍然对牛顿力学感兴趣的作家称为“牛顿主义作家”。这种对用法的诉诸，或许确实能够解释福柯对马克思和弗洛伊德这些被称为“作者”的角色——他们的名字在普莱特的课堂上可能会被热烈提及——的文本遗产的理解，即他们分别代表了马克思主义和弗洛伊德主义的话语领域。从某种意义上说，这或许强化了福柯的论点，即“马克思”和“弗洛伊德”是辩论和思想发展的特殊开端，这种发展并不必然屈从于其创始人的影响。这当然值得商榷；诚然，许多人将马克思和弗洛伊德视为暴君，但在他们所创立的传统框架内，完全可以理解为他们是思维方式的启蒙者，而非这些思维方式的权威主导者。无论如何，这正是福柯想要保留给那些他称之为“话语奠基人”的特殊人物的范畴。

Foucault is concerned also to distinguish figures like Marx and Freud from scientists like Galileo and Newton. In defense of Foucault here, notice that whereas we speak of people as Marxist or Freudian, we don’t speak of people as Radcliffeian or Galilean or Newtonian. We use the adjective “Newtonian” in just the author-neutral way that Poulet used such terms in my anecdote, but we don’t speak of writers who are still interested in Newtonian mechanics as “Newtonian writers.” This appeal to usage may indeed justify Foucault’s understanding of the textual legacy of those author functions known as Marx and Freud—whose names might be raised in Poulet’s lecture class with an enthusiastic response—as placeholders for Marxist and Freudian fields of discourse. It may, in some sense, reinforce Foucault’s argument that “Marx” and “Freud” are special inaugurations of debate, of developing thought, that does not necessarily cringe under the influence of the originary figure. That’s certainly debatable; of course there are a great many people who think of Marx and Freud as tyrants, but within the traditions that they established, it is quite possible to understand them as instigating ways of thinking without necessarily presiding over those ways of thinking authoritatively. That in any case is the special category that Foucault wants to reserve for those privileged figures whom he calls founders of discursivity.

那么，我们可以迅速得出结论：作者之死以及作者功能被简化为作者功能，其后果之一，正如福柯在书中略带讽刺地提及（907），是作者“没有法律地位”。什么？版权呢？知识产权呢？说作者没有法律地位，岂不是把我们带回了十八世纪？然而，请再次注意福柯完全了解的知识背景。版权作为一种资产阶级观念而出现，它允许我宣称我拥有我的作品，我是它的所有者。作者的消失，与资产阶级思想本身的消失相一致，实际上意味着版权或知识产权概念的消亡。在福柯的时代，让-吕克·戈达尔通过不再担任导演（作者）并隐居于电影公社来表明这一点。因此，福柯关于作者没有法律地位的论述，终究是前后一致的。

Very quickly then to conclude: one consequence of the death of the author and the reduction of the author to author function is, as Foucault curiously says in passing (907), that the author “has no legal status.” What? What about copyright? What about intellectual property? Surely to say that the author has no legal status puts us back in the eighteenth century. Notice once again, however, the intellectual context of which Foucault is fully aware. Copyright arose as a bourgeois idea, allowing me to say that I possess my writing, I am its owner. The disappearance of the author, in keeping with the disappearance of bourgeois thought itself, entails, in fact, setting aside notions of copyright or intellectual property. In Foucault’s time, Jean-Luc Godard made this point in ceasing to be director (auteur) and disappearing into film communes. So there is after all consistency in what Foucault is saying about the author having no legal status.

但或许现在真的是时候坚持立场了。“我是一位拉丁裔女同性恋者。我以作家的身份站在你们面前，阐述我的身份，发出我的声音，目的是为了获得自由；不是为了约束你们，不是为了剥夺你们的自由，而是为了获得我自己的自由。我以作家的身份，自豪地站在你们面前。我不想被称作‘作家工具’。我不想被称作某种超越我自身的力量的工具，因为坦白说，我一直都是如此。而现在，我拥有了作为作家的权威，我想提醒你们，我不是任何人的工具，我是自主的，是自由的。”

But maybe at this point it really is time to dig in our heels. “I am a lesbian Latina. I stand before you as an author articulating an identity and finding a voice for the purpose of achieving freedom; not to police you, not to deny your freedom, but to find my own freedom. I stand before you, in pride, as an author. I don’t want to be called an author function. I don’t want to be called an instrument of something larger than myself because frankly that’s what I’ve always been, and now, invested in the authority of my authorship, I want to remind you that I am not anybody’s instrument but that I am autonomous and free.”

传统的作者观念——姑且称之为家长式观念——在福柯和巴特20世纪60年代末的著作中备受质疑——显然可以这样颠覆。它可以被理解为一种新近获得的权威的来源，一种刚刚获得解放、渴望被读者群体理解的自由的来源。我们很难预料福柯会如何回应；而由此引出的问题也暴露出一个困扰着我们接下来讲座内容的难题——尤其是在那些被称为文化研究、关注身份政治的理论领域。在这些学科内部，存在着一种思想分歧：一方肯定所讨论身份的自主完整性和个体性，另一方则认为任何身份都只是“主体位置”——简而言之，就是功能——它们通过社会实践的矩阵得以展现。这种分歧也存在于那些并非直接涉及身份政治的理论形式之中。迟早会在那些重视发现自主主体性的人和那些重视在任何和所有主体位置的不稳定性中发现自我消解或摆脱自我意识的人之间产生争论。

The traditional idea of the author, call it a paternalistic idea—so much under suspicion in the work of Foucault and Barthes in the late 1960s—can obviously be turned on its ear in this way. It can be understood as a source of newfound authority, of the freedom of one who is only recently liberated and hopes to be received by a reading community with that understanding. It’s hard to know how a Foucault might respond; and the issues entailed bring to the surface a problem that dogs much of what we’re going to read during the course of these lectures—even and especially within the sorts of theorizing that are called cultural studies and concern the politics of identity. Within those disciplines there is a division of thought between people who affirm the autonomous integrity and individuality of the identity in question and those who say any and all identities are only “subject positions”—functions, in short—that are revealed through the matrix of social practices. This same split exists, too, within those forms of theory that don’t directly have to do with the politics of identity. A dispute arises sooner or later between those for whom what’s important is the discovery of autonomous subjectivity and those for whom what’s important is the discovery of an effacement of the ego or freedom from selfhood within the very instability of any and all subject positions.

以上就是这些入门讲座的全部内容，我们浅尝辄止地探讨了一些关键主题，这些主题我们之后还会反复提及。下一讲我们将转向一个更为明确的主题：诠释学，诠释学的本质，以及我们如何思考相互冲突的诠释学前提所带来的后果。我们的主要文本将是汉斯-格奥尔格·伽达默尔的节选，以及马丁·海德格尔和E·D·赫希的部分段落。

So much then for these introductory lectures, which have touched lightly on key topics that we’ll keep circling back to. In the next lecture we’ll turn to a more sharply delineated subject matter: hermeneutics, what hermeneutics is, and how we can think about the consequences of conflicting hermeneutic premises. Our primary texts will be the excerpt from Hans-Georg Gadamer and a few passages from Martin Heidegger and E. D. Hirsch.

 

 

关于诠释与阅读的初步思考

First Reflections on Interpretation and Reading

 

 

第三章

CHAPTER 3

进入和退出诠释学循环的途径
Ways In and Out of the Hermeneutic Circle

阅读材料：

Readings:

伽达默尔，汉斯-格奥尔格。“理解的历史性提升到诠释学原则的地位。”载《批判传统》，第 721-737 页。

Gadamer, Hans-Georg. “The Elevation of the Historicality of Understanding to the Status of Hermeneutic Principle.” In The Critical Tradition, pp. 721–737.

摘自马丁·海德格尔，ED Hirsch。

Passages from Martin Heidegger, E. D. Hirsch.

尽管“诠释学”这个词听起来有些吓人，但它其实很容易定义，就是解释的科学。你可能会认为诠释学一直都是人们感兴趣的领域，但事实上，它持续受到关注的时间并不长。亚里士多德确实写过一部名为《论解释》（De Interpretatione）的著作，中世纪也十分关注解释，所以我想说的是，当时“诠释学”这个词还没有出现；但同样不可否认的是，在很多时候，人们并不认为应该对我们如何解释事物进行系统的研究。

Despite the intimidating sound of the word, “hermeneutics” is easily defined as the science of interpretation. You would think hermeneutics had always been a matter of interest, but in fact it’s of continuous interest only fairly recently. Aristotle did write a treatise called De Interpretatione, and the Middle Ages were much concerned with interpretation, so I suppose what I’m saying in part is that the word “hermeneutics” wasn’t then available; but it’s also true that at many times the idea that there ought to be a systematic study of how we interpret things wasn’t a matter of pressing concern.

尽管塔木德传统中早已涌现出许多卓越的诠释成就，但在西方世界催生所谓“诠释学”的却是新教改革。我认为这其中蕴含着深刻的意义，我会尝试解释原因，因为在这个历史事实的核心，我们可以找到人们有时重视诠释，有时又漠不关心的原因。只有当（a）意义对你而言变得极其重要，并且（b）理解意义变得困难时，你才会真正开始思考诠释的方法、如何判断诠释的有效性等等。你可能会问自己，意义是否总是重要且难以理解？嗯，并非总是如此。如果你所信奉的圣经由教皇和偶尔召开的教会长老会议来裁决，那么你本人其实无需过多操心圣经的含义。因为你已经被告知了它的含义。但随着新教改革的到来，人们与圣经的关系变得更加私人化，每个人都在牧师的指导下参与到理解圣经的进程​​中——毕竟，圣经本身就相当晦涩难懂（谁又能真正理解那些比喻的含义呢？——而且整本圣经都充满了诠释上的难题）——那么，如何解读经文的担忧自然而然地就变得普遍起来。毋庸置疑，既然圣经是你的神圣文本，它的意义对你来说就至关重要。了解它究竟是什么意思，以及为什么它的意义如此重要，对你来说至关重要。

Although there had long been prodigious feats of interpretation in the Talmudic tradition, what gave rise in the Western world to what is called “hermeneutics” was the Protestant Reformation. There’s a lot of significance in that, I think, and I’ll try to explain why, because at the heart of this historical fact we can find the reason why people care about interpretation at some times and don’t care about it at others. You don’t really puzzle your head about approaches to interpretation, how we determine the validity of interpretation and so on, until (a) meaning becomes terribly important to you, and (b) the ascertainment of meaning becomes difficult. You may ask yourself whether it isn’t always the case that meaning is important and that meaning is hard to construe. Well, not necessarily. If you are a person whose sacred scripture is adjudicated by the pope and the occasional tribunal of church elders, you yourself don’t really need to worry very much about what scripture means. You are told what it means. But in the wake of the Protestant Reformation, when one’s relationship with the Bible became personal and everyone was engaged—with the guidance of their minister—in understanding what is after all pretty difficult stuff (who on earth knows what the parables mean?—and the whole of the Bible poses interpretative problems), then of course worries about how to interpret scripture become prevalent. Needless to say, since it’s your sacred text, the meaning of it is important to you. It’s crucial to you to know exactly what it means and why what it means is important.

随着新教的传播，诠释学思想也随之兴起，人们开始撰写诠释方面的论著——但这些论著始终都指向《圣经》的诠释。换言之，在诠释学中，宗教占据首要地位，因为对普通信徒而言，理解圣经是唯一至关重要的文本。然而，不久之后，宪政民主政体开始出现，人们——无论是作为公民、作为拥有选举权的人，还是作为享有国家或民族赋予的权利的人——都开始更加关注他们所处法律体系的本质。正因如此，诠释学逐渐从宗教领域扩展到法律研究。那些在诠释圣经的过程中发展起来的原则，随后被应用于诠释其他意义几乎同样重要的事物。当然，您也知道，时至今日，诠释学在法律研究中仍然不可或缺：例如，理解宪法的意义的基础是什么？关于这个问题存在广泛的争议，而法学院的许多课程正是为了调解这些争议而开设的。因此，我们再次看到，当某个领域的基础性文献的意义对读者群体而言变得比以往任何时候都更加重要，并且这种意义被认为难以理解时，诠释学便会介入该领域。

So as Protestantism gained currency, by the same token thinking about hermeneutics took hold, and people began to write treatises about interpretation—but it was always interpretation of the Bible. In other words, in hermeneutics, religion came first because for the laity sacred texts were the only texts that it was crucial to understand. Soon enough, though, constitutional democracies began to appear, and when that happened people became much more interested—as citizens or as persons with suffrage or as persons with rights conferred by a state or nation—they became much more interested in the nature of the laws they lived under. That’s why hermeneutics gradually expanded beyond religion to the study of the law. The governing principles that had been developed in thinking about interpreting scripture were then applied to the interpretation of something the meaning of which had become almost as important. You know of course that hermeneutics is inescapable in the study of the law to this day: what are the grounds for understanding the meaning of the Constitution, for example? There are widespread controversies about it, and many of the courses you would take in law school are meant to arbitrate among them. So once again you see that hermeneutics enters a field when the meaning of the foundational documents in that field becomes more important to a community of readers than it had been before and when that meaning is recognized to be difficult to grasp.

我们至今尚未谈及文学，而事实上，（在中世纪人们热衷于阅读世俗文本，尤其是希腊罗马文本，因为宗教寓言逐渐消亡之后）在近代早期和十八世纪的大部分时间里，并没有专门针对文学的诠释学。想想你所研究过的十八世纪作家。令人惊讶的是，他们都理所当然地认为意义是显而易见的。例如，亚历山大·蒲柏，甚至塞缪尔·约翰逊，在思考文学及其重要性以及文学的本质时，很少关注诠释。他们更关注的是评价，确立诗歌应有的形态和应达成的目标，并在过程中提出一些主要涉及道德和美学的问题。他们不关心诠释，因为在他们看来，好的写作就是清晰明了、意义透明，无需诠释的写作。事实上，在这一时期，剧作家们都在为自己的剧作撰写序言，互相抨击对方晦涩难懂——也就是说，互相抨击对方需要解读。“我不明白你的比喻到底是什么意思。你根本不知道什么是比喻。你只会一个接一个地犯错。没人能理解你。”这几乎是十八世纪戏剧作品散文和诗歌序言中反复出现的主题。由此可见，解读不仅无人研究，而且被认为毫无必要，除非你想读的是劣质文学。如果需要解读，那它就称不上好。

As yet we haven’t said anything about literature, and the fact is that (after the medieval preoccupation with reading secular texts, especially the Greek and Roman ones, as religious allegory had died away) there was no hermeneutic art devoted to literature during the early modern period and for most of the eighteenth century. Think about the writers you’ve studied from the eighteenth century. It’s striking that they all just take meaning for granted. Alexander Pope, for example, and even Samuel Johnson reflect on literature and why it’s important and what the nature of literature is without much concern for interpretation. They’re concerned instead with evaluation, establishing the principles of what a poem should be like and try to accomplish, while raising questions along the way that are largely moral and aesthetic. They are not concerned about interpretation because to them good writing is writing that’s unambiguously clear, writing the meaning of which is so transparent that it doesn’t need to be interpreted. In fact, during this whole period playwrights were writing prologues to their plays abusing each other for being obscure—that is, abusing each other for requiring interpretation. “I don’t understand what your metaphors are all about. You don’t know what a metaphor is. All you do is make one verbal mistake after another. Nobody can understand you.” This is the recurrent topic of the prose and verse prefaces to theatrical pieces in the eighteenth century, and from that you can see that interpretation is not only not studied but is considered unnecessary unless you wish to read bad literature. If you have to interpret it, it isn’t any good.

随着十八世纪的推进，浪漫主义兴起——这一点众所周知，而且我认为常常被过分夸大——一种天才崇拜也随之出现。在这一时期，人们认为最优秀的作品源于作者非凡的思维敏锐度或精神洞察力。随着对超凡想象力的强调，文学创作者开始被视为神圣的创造者，并在某种程度上成为神圣创造者的化身。要知道，西方文化的世俗化在启蒙运动时期——也就是整个十八世纪——都在不断加剧，随着某些圈子中神圣经典地位的下降，文学天才之作开始与之抗衡。诺思罗普·弗莱将浪漫主义时期的典型作品称为“世俗经典”。这类文学作品的意义变得更加难以理解——正如那些研读过布莱克和雪莱作品的人所能体会到的——因为它带有浓厚的个人色彩，不再反映出蒲柏时代那些“常被思考却从未被充分表达”的文学作品所秉持的共同价值观。因此，在浪漫主义时期，随着文学至少在一定程度上开始取代宗教的角色，意义的重要性和理解的难度都随之增加，而此时，文学诠释学便显得尤为必要。

Then as the eighteenth century wears on, with the emergence of Romanticism—as is well known and I think often overstated—there emerges a cult of genius. At this period, the best work is said to arise from the extraordinary mental acuity or spiritual insight of the author. And with this new emphasis on the transcendent faculty of imagination, the literary creator starts to seem like the divine creator and to a certain extent becomes a placeholder for the divine creator. Remember that secularization in Western culture was increasing during the course of the Enlightenment—during the course of the eighteenth century—and as sacred scripture in some circles receded in importance, works of literary genius began to rival it. Northrop Frye has called the characteristic work of the Romantic period a “secular scripture.” The meaning of this sort of literature has become more difficult—as those of you who have tackled Blake and Shelley can attest—because it is deeply personal and no longer reflects the shared values that had made for the literature of “what oft was thought but ne’er so well exprest” in the age of Pope. Thus in the Romantic period, both the importance of meaning and the difficulty of meaning increased as literature began at least partly for some readers to take over the role of religion, and at that point a literary hermeneutics became necessary.

浪漫主义时期的神学家弗里德里希·施莱尔马赫毕生致力于一种诠释学方法，这种方法既适用于文学研究，也适用于圣经研究。他的著作确立了一种以文学为诠释学核心的传统。紧随施莱尔马赫之后的是世纪之交的威廉·狄尔泰、 1927年出版的《存在与时间》中的马丁·海德格尔以及伽达默尔。此外，还有一种与之竞争的传统，它从康德经由胡塞尔传承至埃米利奥·贝蒂和E·D·赫希，我们将在适当的时候探讨赫希与伽达默尔之间的争论。

A theologian of the Romantic period, Friedrich Schleiermacher, devoted his career to an approach to hermeneutics that was meant to be applied as much to literature as to the study of scripture, and his work established a tradition in which literature was a central concern in hermeneutic thought. What followed directly from Schleiermacher was the work of Wilhelm Dilthey around the turn of the century, of Martin Heidegger in his Being and Time of 1927, and of Gadamer. There is a rival tradition that descends from Kant through Husserl to Emilio Betti and E. D. Hirsch, and we shall consider Hirsch’s quarrel with Gadamer in due course.

那么，施莱尔马赫传统下诠释学的基本问题是什么呢？或许你们都听说过“诠释循环”。它描述了读者与文本之间的关系，或者——在某些诠释学学者看来，但并非伽达默尔的观点——描述了读者与作者之间的关系。例如，赫希认为诠释循环是读者与作者之间的关系，文本是一种指向作者意图的中介性文件。但对于伽达默尔及其传统而言，循环的概念截然不同，这一点我们将在阐述伽达默尔对“浪漫主义”或许令人惊讶的态度时看到。不过，与此同时，所有人都会认同，读者与文本或作者之间的循环关系可以用多种方式来描述。它通常被描述为部分与整体之间的关系，而循环性问题正是由此而来：当我阅读一篇文本时，我首先读到的当然是一个短语或一个句子。文本还有很多，所以第一个片段只是其中的一部分。但我立刻开始基于一个想象的或假定的整体来形成对这部分的看法，这种看法要么是我从这部分投射出来的，要么是我在初读之前就已经有的。然后，我运用这种对整体的感知来继续阅读后续的部分——无论是行、句，还是其他任何部分。我不断地将这些后续部分与对整体的感知联系起来，而这种感知最终会随着对部分了解的加深而改变。这种阐释过程的循环往复在于：从一个部分出发，形成对整体的预设，再回到下一个部分，再回到对整体的修正感知，如此循环往复。

So what is the basic problematic for hermeneutics in the tradition of Schleiermacher? Probably you have all heard of the “hermeneutic circle.” It describes the relationship between a reader and a text or—in the view of certain students of hermeneutics but not that of Gadamer—of a relationship between a reader and an author. Hirsch, for example, thinks the hermeneutic circle is a relationship between a reader and an author, with the text a kind of a mediatory document pointing toward the meaning of the author. But for Gadamer and his tradition, the circle is very differently conceived, as we shall see when I point out Gadamer’s perhaps surprising attitude toward “romanticism.” In the meantime, though, all would agree that the circular relationship between a reader and a text or author can be described in a variety of ways. It’s often put in terms of the relationship between the part and the whole, and here is how the problematic of circularity enters into it: I approach a text and of course the first thing I read is a phrase or a sentence. There’s still a lot more of the text and so that first fragment is a part, but I immediately begin to form an opinion about this part based on an imagined or supposed whole, an opinion that I project from this part or else possess in advance of this initial reading. I then use this sense of what the whole must be like to continue to read successive parts—lines, sentences, whatever they may be. I keep referring those successive parts back to a sense of the whole, which after all changes as a result of knowing more and more of the parts. The circularity of this interpretative engagement involves moving from a part to a preconception about the whole, back to the next part, back to a revised sense of the whole, and so on in a circular pattern.

这种循环性也可以理解为现在与过去之间的一种互动——在我特定的历史视野与我试图理解的其他历史视野之间的互动。我将我对世界的认知运用到对文本的解读中；我思考文本似乎在表达的内容与我已有的知识之间的关系，同时允许文本通过传递其自身的知识来修正我的认知。最后，诠释学不仅仅是跨越历史鸿沟的桥梁——它也可以跨越社会或文化鸿沟，甚至可能跨越并不大的鸿沟——因此，即使我们只是进行对话，我们仍然在进行诠释行为。我必须努力理解你的意思，并将我对你信息的解读与我想要表达的内容联系起来，我们之间的沟通渠道必须保持畅通，以确保我们对所谈论的内容形成并不断发展的相互理解。更明显的是，跨文化对话也是如此。因此，诠释学并非总是关乎伽达默尔所说的历史视野的融合。它还关乎社会、文化和人际关系视野的融合。所有这些都包含在伽达默尔所说的“视野融合”（Horizo​​ntverschmelzung）的含义之中。

This circularity can also be understood as an interchange between the present and the past—between my particular historical horizon and some other historical horizon that I’m trying to come to terms with. I bring what I know about the world to bear on my engagement with the text; I consider what the text seems to be saying in relation to what I already knew while allowing the text to modify my knowledge by imparting its own. Finally, because hermeneutics isn’t just a bridge across a historical gulf—because it also can come into play across a social or cultural gulf, maybe not even very much of a gulf—we are still performing a hermeneutic act when we simply engage each other in conversation. I have to try to understand what you’re saying, referring my interpretation of your message to what I want to say, and the circuit of communication between us has to stay open to ensure a mutual and developing understanding of what we’re talking about. It’s the same thing, more obviously, with conversations across cultures. So hermeneutics doesn’t always concern what Gadamer would call merging historical horizons. It’s also about merging social and cultural and interpersonal horizons as well. All of that is entailed in what Gadamer means by Horizontverschmelzung.

以下是伽达默尔对这种思维循环运作方式的解释（722）：

Here is Gadamer’s version of how the circularity of this thinking works (722):

[读者——伽达默尔用“他”来指代——]一旦文本中出现某种初始意义，便会预先设想文本整体的意义。[换句话说，一旦他看到文本的某个部分是什么样子，他就会设想或想象包含该部分的整体应该是什么样子。]再次强调，后者（即初始意义的意义）的出现，仅仅是因为读者带着对某种特定意义的预期来阅读文本。这种预先设想（即我们预先对即将阅读的内容的意义所抱有的预感）的实现，会随着读者深入理解文本意义的过程而不断修正，最终形成对文本意义的理解。
[The reader—Gadamer’s word is “he”] projects before himself a meaning for the text as a whole as soon as some initial meaning emerges in the text. [In other words, as soon as he sees what the part is like, he projects or imagines what the whole must be that contains this part.] Again the latter [that is, the sense of the initial meaning] emerges only because he is reading the text with particular expectations in regard to a certain meaning. The working out of this fore-project [that is, the sense we have in advance of the meaning of what we are going to read], which is constantly revised in terms of what emerges as he penetrates into the meaning, is understanding what is there.

“存在之物”是伽达默尔从海德格尔那里继承的一个表达，它与伽达默尔经常谈到的“主题”（ die Sache）的含义相符。换句话说，读者理解文本意义的努力，就是掌握主题，即“存在之物”的努力：我想，用通俗易懂的方式来说，就是“文本的真正意义是什么”。

“What is there” is an expression that Gadamer inherits from Heidegger, and it corresponds with what Gadamer means when he frequently talks about die Sache, the “subject matter.” In other words, the effort a reader makes in coming to terms with the meaning of a text is an effort to master the subject matter, what is there: I suppose it would be fair enough to say, as a colloquial paraphrase, “what the text is really about.”

总之，你可以看出，伽达默尔在这段文字中对我们阅读循环性的描述可能会引发一些担忧。他反复强调“先验结构”、“先验计划”、“先验认知”，这让我们不禁停下来思考。难道我不能客观地看待“文本本身”吗？换句话说，如果我对文本的意义抱有某种先入为主的观念，我岂不是会无可救药地带有偏见？为什么我不能抛开这些先入为主的观念，尤其是在文本不断揭示更多信息的情况下，以便准确理解文本的真正含义？即便文本不断揭示更多信息，如果你告诉我，每一次因进一步阅读而产生的思维修正，最终都会变成另一个先验计划或先验观念，那我又该如何理解文本的真正含义呢？

Anyway, you can see that in this passage Gadamer is describing the circularity of our reading in a way that may raise some concerns. We are given pause, here and elsewhere, by his harping on “fore-structure,” “fore-project,” “fore-having.” Can’t I view “what is there,” as we might say, objectively? In other words, won’t I be hopelessly prejudiced about what I read if I’ve got some sort of preliminary conception of what its meaning is? Why can’t I just set aside my preliminary conceptions, especially as the text tells me more and more, so that I can understand precisely what is there? Even given that the text tells me more and more, how am I ever going to understand what is there if you tell me that each revision of what I think as a result of further reading nevertheless becomes in itself yet another fore-project or preliminary conception?

当海德格尔和伽达默尔坚持认为，尽管我们总是在先入为主的观念框架内进行诠释——正如我们将看到的，伽达默尔大胆地称之为“偏见”——但正如海德格尔所说，进入圆的路径仍然有两种，一种是好的，一种是坏的。换句话说，圆未必是一个恶性循环，如果你无法摆脱先入为主的观念，你很可能会得出这样的结论。伽达默尔和海德格尔坚持认为，进入圆的路径也可以是“建设性的”。

This claim is especially difficult to credit when Heidegger and Gadamer then insist that even though we always interpret within our preliminary conceptions—Gadamer boldly calls them “prejudices,” as we’ll see—there nevertheless are, as Heidegger puts it, two ways into the circle, a good way and a bad way. A circle, in other words, is not necessarily a vicious circle, as you are tempted to conclude it is if you can’t escape preconceptions. Gadamer and Heidegger insist that the way into the circle can also be “constructive.”

为了理解这一论断，请看附录中海德格尔的第二段文字，仅看第一句，他写道：“在诠释中，我们所诠释的实体应如何被理解，可以从实体本身得出；或者，诠释也可以将实体强加于与其存在方式相悖的概念之中。”你或许会问，如果你被先入为主的观念所束缚，又如何能“从实体本身”得出任何东西呢？好吧，让我举个例子来佐证海德格尔的区分。十八世纪，一位名叫马克·阿肯赛德的诗人写了一篇名为《想象的乐趣》（1744）的长篇诗文，其中有一句描写“世界的至高精神”举起“他那可塑的手臂”。¹我们现代读者对聚合物很熟悉。我们知道塑料是什么。仅从我们自身的认知范围来看，我们毫不犹豫地得出结论：造物主举起的是一条假肢。但毕竟，我们对阿肯赛德创作这首诗时的视野还是有所了解的：我们知道，在十八世纪，“plastic”一词的意思是“蜿蜒的”、“强大的”、“灵活的”，所以我们可以打开我们封闭的视野，得出结论：伟大的创造者举起了他蜿蜒、强大、灵活的手臂——我们不禁注意到，这更有道理。

To understand this claim, take a look in the appendix at the second passage from Heidegger, just the first sentence of it, where he says, “In an interpretation, the way in which the entity we are interpreting is to be conceived can be drawn from the entity itself, or the interpretation can force the entity into concepts to which it is opposed in its manner of being.” You might well ask how you can draw anything “from the entity itself” if you are trapped in preconceptions. Well, let me give you an example in support of Heidegger’s distinction. In the eighteenth century, a poet named Mark Akenside wrote a long verse essay called The Pleasures of the Imagination (1744), where you will find a line about the “The Sovereign spirit of the world” raising “his plastic arm.”1 We modern readers are into polymers. We know what plastic is. Strictly from within our own horizons we don’t hesitate to conclude that the creator raised a prosthetic limb. But, after all, we do know something about the horizon within which Akenside was writing his poem: we are aware that in the eighteenth century the word “plastic” meant “sinuous,” “powerful,” “flexible,” so we can open our closed horizon and conclude that the great creator raised his sinuous, powerful, flexible arm—which, we can’t help noticing, makes a lot more sense.

这就是良性偏见和不良偏见的区别。良性偏见是指我们事先意识到——尽管它仍然是一种“偏见”（Vorurteil，预判）——塑料的含义已经发生了变化。不良偏见则是指我们想都没想就断定塑料是一种聚合物，完全没有考虑过可能存在其他历史背景。如果我们援引十八世纪的含义，就会立刻发现这句话完全合理；但如果我们用自己的理解来解释，就不得不承认这句话是无稽之谈。

Here you have the difference between good and bad prejudice. The good prejudice is our prior awareness—still a “prejudice” (Vorurteil, prejudgment)—that plastic has changed its meaning. The bad prejudice is when we leap to the conclusion, without thinking for a moment that there might be some other historical horizon, that plastic is a polymer. If we invoke the eighteenth-century meaning, we immediately see that the line makes perfect sense; but if we bring our own meaning to bear, we have to admit that the line is nonsense.

稍后在阅读W.K. Wimsatt的论文《意图谬误》时，我会再次提及这个例子。届时，我会提出这样一种可能性：假设世界的创造者举起了他的假肢，或许确实具有一定的价值。但就目前而言，你应该明白，这是一种很好的方式，可以帮助我们理解在解释行为中，有用的预设和无用的预设之间的区别。

I’ll come back to this example later on when we read an essay called “The Intentional Fallacy” by W. K. Wimsatt, and I will then raise the possibility that there might actually be some value in supposing that the creator of the world raised his prosthetic limb. But for the moment it should be plain to you that this is a good way of understanding what the difference between a useful preconception and a useless preconception brought to bear on an interpretative act might consist in.

现在，我举的例子有点跑题了，所以让我先回顾一下，补充一些细节。正如你从阅读伽达默尔的著作中——以及从这段摘录出自的伟大著作《真理与方法》 （Wahrheit und Methode）的标题中——所了解到的那样，这个标题隐含地暗示了真理与方法之间的区别——伽达默尔对其他人诠释学方法的主要反对意见在于，他们认为存在一种诠释方法论。在你读到的这段摘录中，伽达默尔抨击的基本方法论就是他所谓的“历史主义”。

Now in giving the example, I’ve gotten a little bit ahead of myself, so let me go back and fill in some blanks. As you can tell from your reading of Gadamer—and also from the title of the great book from which this excerpt is taken, Truth and Method (Wahrheit und Methode), with its implicit suggestion that there is a difference between truth and method—as you can tell, the great objection of Gadamer to other people’s way of doing hermeneutics is that they believe there is a methodology of interpretation. The basic methodology Gadamer is attacking in the excerpt you’ve read is what he calls “historicism.”

“历史主义”这个词对我们来说很复杂，因为在课程的后续部分，我们将探讨新历史主义，它与伽达默尔在此反对的内容几乎没有任何关系。伽达默尔所说的“历史主义”是指这样一种信念：你可以抛开先入之见，彻底排除自身的主观性，排除自身对事物的看法，从而进入另一个时代或地点的思维模式：你可以完全进入另一个人的思维，将自己的思维抛诸脑后。这就是实现“历史客观性”的“方法”，正如我们将在本讲结尾看到的那样，它具有某种高贵的特质，应该与伽达默尔诠释学的高贵特质并置。伽达默尔反对这种意义上的历史主义，首先是因为他认为这是不可能的。你不可能排除先入之见。你所能做的，就是承认另一个视野的存在，而不是试图“框定”或完全搁置自己的视野——这几乎是不可能的。你要努力寻找共同点，找到某种方式将现在与过去、此地与彼地融合起来，这或许能促成伽达默尔所说的“视野融合”。视野融合的积极成果，正是伽达默尔所说的“有效历史”，他指的是有用的历史——真正能为我们服务的历史，我们可以从中学习的历史，而不仅仅是客观地记录过去的档案。伽达默尔还认为，即使历史主义本身是可行的，它也存在某种不道德之处，因为它对过去抱有居高临下的姿态，假定过去仅仅是信息的储存库，却忘记了它或许能教会我们一些东西。我们最后会回到这一点。

“Historicism” is a complicated word for us because later in the course we’re going to be exploring the New Historicism, which has nothing to do, or very little, with what Gadamer is objecting to here. What Gadamer means by “historicism” is the belief that you can set aside preconceptions, that you can completely factor out your own subjectivity, your own view of things, in order to enter into the mindset of some other time or place: that you can completely enter another mind, leaving your own behind. This is the “method” of achieving “historical objectivity,” and as we’ll see at the end of this lecture, there’s a certain nobility about it that should be juxtaposed with the nobility of Gadamerian hermeneutics. Gadamer objects to historicism in this sense in the first place because he thinks it’s impossible. You cannot factor out preconceptions. All you can do is acknowledge another horizon without attempting the impossible feat of “bracketing” or setting aside your own horizon altogether. You try to find common ground, to find some way of merging a present with a past, a here with a there, which can result in what Gadamer calls, again, “horizon merger.” The positive result of horizon merger is what Gadamer calls “effective history,” by which he means history that is useful—history that really can go to work for us, history from which we can learn, not just an archive that objectifies the past. Gadamer also thinks that there’s something immoral about historicism, even if it were possible, because it condescends toward the past, presuming that the past is simply a repository of information and forgetting that it may have something to teach us. We’ll return to this point in the end.

或许为了使这种观点显得合情合理，我们应该稍作反思。毕竟，我们大多数人都为自己的客观性能力感到自豪，不愿动摇我们“搁置”偏见（正如胡塞尔所说）并如实地看待过去或任何其他形式的“他者”的信念。因此，让我们来看看海德格尔在《存在与时间》中对“诠释学循环”的分析中的几段文字，看看海德格尔对这一论断有何看法。首先：

Perhaps in order to make this viewpoint seem plausible, we should study it more reflectively for a moment. After all, most of us are proud of our capacity for objectivity and don’t wish to be shaken in our conviction that we can “bracket” our prejudices (as Husserl would say) and view the past or any other form of otherness for what it is. So let’s look at a couple of passages from Heidegger’s “analytic of the hermeneutic circle” in Being and Time, to see what Heidegger has to say about this claim. First:

当我们与任何事物打交道时，仅仅是看到离我们最近的事物，就本身蕴含着解释的结构，而且这种结构是如此原始，以至于仅仅为了抓住某种摆脱了“作为”的事物，就需要进行某种调整。
When we have to do with anything, the mere seeing of the things which are closest to us bears in itself the structure of interpretation and in so primordial a manner that just to grasp something free, as it were, of the “as” requires a certain adjustment.

海德格尔到底在说什么？我来做一个思想实验。我看向房间后方，看到一个写着“出口”的标志。我没有解读它，也没有任何先入为主的观念。我只是在看。但是等等，我怎么知道它是一个标志？我怎么知道它写的是“出口”？我把无数的先入为主的观念强加到我原本以为只是简单的“看”这个行为上。海德格尔承认，想象“仅仅看到”某物而不把它看作“某物”（仿佛“摆脱了‘作为’”）的可能性并非毫无意思。仅仅拥有眼前之物或许令人兴奋。但他认为这几乎是不可能的。要忘记我正在看一个写着“出口”的标志，而只是去看“那里有什么”，却不知道它是什么，这是一种非常困难的心理活动。换句话说，我并非一开始就不知道那是一个写着“出口”的标志。可能存在感官刺激，但此前并无意识活动。我最先知道的，无论准确与否，都是某个物体是某种特定的事物，而不是其他事物。

What is Heidegger saying? Let me try a thought experiment. I look to the back of the room, where I see that sign that says “exit.” I’m not interpreting it. I don’t have any preconception about it. I’m just looking. But wait. How do I know it’s a sign? How do I know it says “exit”? I bring a thousand preconceptions to bear on what I take to be a simple act of looking. Heidegger concedes that it’s not at all uninteresting to imagine the possibility of “just seeing” something without seeing it as something (“free, as it were, of the ‘as’ ”). It might be exhilarating just to have something before us. But he thinks that is well nigh impossible. It is a very difficult mental act to forget that I am looking at a sign that says “exit” and just to look at “what is there” without knowing what it is. In other words, I don’t not know first that that’s a sign that says “exit.” There may be sensory stimulus but there is no prior act of consciousness. The very first thing I know, whether accurately or not, is that an object is some particular thing and not something else.

正如海德格尔所指出的，看似原始的“仅仅拥有眼前之物”的时刻，如果真能被体验到的话，源于对先入之见的遗忘。我总是已经对所观察的任何对象有所诠释，但这绝非意味着我的诠释是正确的。这仅仅意味着我无法回避这样一个事实：心灵的最初运动——而非最终的运动，而是心灵的最初运动——本身就具有诠释性。继续这段话：“这种摆脱了‘如’的把握，是一种对那种仅仅理解的观看方式的剥夺[你可以看出海德格尔对此有多么着迷，因为他改变了他的修辞]。”简而言之，不理解将是一种非凡的体验。理解本身是一种囚禁，当海德格尔说不必仅仅理解会令人兴奋时，他也在强调，这是一种极其困难，甚至是不可能的思维扭曲。所以，这就是为什么我们必须认识到，当我们做翻译时（我们总是翻译，在我们生活的每一刻都是翻译），我们总是带着先入为主的观念和“偏见”在工作。

As Heidegger points out, then, the seemingly primordial moment of “just having something before us,” if it can be experienced at all, derives from the forgetting of preconceptions. I am always already in possession of an interpretation of whatever object I look at, which isn’t at all to say that my interpretation is correct. It’s only to say that I can’t escape the fact that the very first movement of mind, not the last movement but the first movement of mind, is interpretative. Continue the passage: “This grasping which is free of the ‘as’ is a privation of the kind of seeing [and you see how attracted Heidegger is to it because he shifts his rhetoric] in which one merely understands.” In short, it would be a remarkable experience not to understand. It’s a kind of imprisonment, understanding, and when Heidegger says that it would be exciting not to have to merely understand, he’s also insisting that this is an incredibly difficult, if not impossible, contortion of thought. So that’s why we must realize that when we are interpreters (and we are always interpreters, every moment of our lives), we are always working with preconceptions, “prejudices.”

那么，伽达默尔所说的“偏见”一词又该如何理解呢？他认为这会冒犯我们的感受，因此对此有所辩解，并深入探讨了其词源。法语的“préjugé”和德语的“Voruteil”都意为“预判”或“先入为主的判断”。他指出，这种意义上的偏见实际上可以在法庭上作为判决过程中的一个阶段。它们不必被视为庸俗的偏见（即以不良方式进入某种圈子的情况）。顺便一提，后者之一便是“反对偏见的偏见”，伽达默尔认为这是欧洲启蒙运动的典型立场——正是这种偏见使其得以宣称客观性。

Now what about Gadamer’s word “prejudice”? He sees that it will be an affront to our sensibilities and is somewhat defensive about it, going into the appropriate etymologies. The French préjugé and the German Voruteil both mean “prejudgment” or “prior judgment.” Prejudices in this sense can actually be used in courts of law, he says, as a stage in the process of arriving at a verdict. They needn’t be thought of as vulgar prejudices (instances of entering the circle in a bad way). One of these latter by the way is the “prejudice against prejudice,” which Gadamer considers the characteristic stance of the European Enlightenment—the prejudice that enables its claim to objectivity.

但偏见是有害的。我们都知道偏见在历史和社会层面造成了怎样的后果，我们怎敢以这种方式为其辩护呢？必须承认，伽达默尔在你读到的这段摘录中所做的事情，至少是一种知识保守主义的行为。他谈论“古典主义”的那一部分乍看之下似乎是离题。然而，我们应该意识到，当他讨论古典主义（他后来称之为“传统”）时，他是在确立自己的观点：除非我们与所读内容拥有非常广泛而深刻的共同基础，否则我们无法有效地融合不同的视野。对伽达默尔而言，古典主义或“传统”的伟大之处在于，他认为它是我们可以共享的东西。伽达默尔认为，古典并非主要针对其特定的历史时期，而是面向所有时代，它以不同的方式与我们所有人对话，但最终都与我们对话，并声称其所言为真理。

But prejudice is harmful. We know what prejudice has wrought historically and socially, so how dare we try to vindicate it in this way? It has to be admitted that what Gadamer does in the excerpt you have read is to perform an act of intellectual conservatism at the least. That whole section of the excerpt in which he talks about “classicism” may seem at first blush to be a digression. We should realize, though, that when he discusses classicism, which he later calls “tradition,” he is establishing his claim that we really can’t merge horizons effectively unless we have a very broad and extensive common ground to share with what we’re reading. The great thing about classicism for Gadamer, or “tradition,” is that he supposes it to be something we can share. The classical, Gadamer argues, is that which doesn’t speak mainly to its own historical moment but speaks for all time, speaks to all of us in different ways but does speak to us, proffering its claim to speak true.

当然，我们意识到，伽达默尔有权拥有一套思想保守的经典体系。他认为，除非人们拥有大量的共同基础，否则他们无法理解过去或他者。但即便我们不必对伽达默尔本人做出任何推断，也可以看出，偏见的“庸俗”和破坏性一面正是在此伺机而动。在伽达默尔称之为古典——即古代——的传统中，许多受人尊敬的人物都认为奴隶制完全合理且自然，这其中也包括许多从未质疑过奴隶制的现代人物。伽达默尔并未提及这一点，尽管政治哲学家和思想史学家经常讨论，但我们意识到，如果一个人不够批判，不够自我疏离，那么他很可能也会认同这种偏见，而这种批判和疏离恰恰体现了共享共同基础的姿态。虽然我们可以清楚地理解“偏见”仅仅是指无法摆脱的先入之见，这是进入诠释学循环的一种可接受的、甚至是必要的途径，但完全放弃我们对偏见的偏见是愚蠢的。

Certainly, we realize, Gadamer is entitled to an intellectually conservative canon. He is not sure people can understand the past or otherness unless they share a great deal of common ground. But without drawing any necessary inferences about Gadamer himself, we can see that right here is where the “vulgar,” destructive aspect of prejudice has a chance to sneak in. Slavery was considered perfectly appropriate and natural to a great many of the most exalted figures working within the tradition that Gadamer rightly calls classical—classical antiquity, including a great many figures of the modern era who never stopped to question slavery. Gadamer doesn’t talk about this, although political philosophers and historians of thought often do, but we recognize that this is an aspect of that prejudice that one might share with tradition if one weren’t somewhat more critical, more self-distancing, than the gesture of sharing common ground might imply. While plainly we can understand “prejudice” simply to mean inescapable preconception, an acceptable and indeed necessary way into the hermeneutic circle, it would be foolish to abandon our prejudice against prejudice altogether.

在接下来的讲座中，我想请大家注意两段文字，一段出自伽达默尔的著作，我即将引用；另一段出自美国学者E·D·赫希的著作，收录于附录的第四段。你们或许知道赫希，他著有一本涵盖所有学童必备知识的词典，也是文学理论蓬勃发展时期知识分子右翼的代表人物。赫希始终是一位认真研究诠释学的学者，他与伽达默尔就诠释原则展开了长期的争论。

What I’d like to do in the rest of this lecture is to call your attention to two passages, one in Gadamer’s text that I’m about to cite and the other the fourth passage in the appendix by an American scholar, E. D. Hirsch, whom you may know as the author of a dictionary of what every school child should know and as a hero of the intellectual right during the whole period when literary theory flourished. Hirsch was always a serious student of hermeneutics and conducted a long-standing feud with Gadamer about the principles of interpretation.

首先，伽达默尔不仅反对历史主义，也反对他所谓的诠释学中的“浪漫主义”，因为正如我之前提到的，浪漫主义关注的是作者的思想。伽达默尔认为，读者应该与文本而非作者相遇，因为他所谓的文本“主题”（die Sache）至少同样属于其历史视野，而非个体思想。与此相反，赫希认为意义是“意识的产物，而非文字的产物”；也就是说，意义既不存在于某个思想史的瞬间，也不存在于仅仅作为文字的文本本身，而是存在于其作者的思想之中。我们稍后会再讨论赫希对“意图”的诉求。

This by way of prelude: Gadamer is opposed not only to historicism but to what he calls “romanticism” in hermeneutics because, as I indicated earlier, romanticism is focused on the mind of the author. Gadamer thinks the encounter of the reader should be with a text, not an author, because what he calls the “subject matter” of the text (die Sache) belongs at least as much to its historical horizon as to an individual mind. Hirsch in contrast thinks that meaning is “an affair of consciousness not of words”; that is, meaning is to be found neither in a moment of intellectual history nor in the words of a text considered simply as words, but in reference to the mind of its author. Hirsch’s appeal to “intention” is a matter to which we’ll soon return.

这两段文字并置呈现了我在描述伽达默尔立场时一直试图阐明的观点。伽达默尔论述的尊严和高贵之处在于，它包含着对“真理”的关注，并始终保持着意义、获得意义以及最终获得某种对我们而言是真理的事物之间可能存在联系的可能性。另一方面，赫希则唤起了一种截然不同的尊严。我希望你们在对比这两段文字时意识到，它们之间无法调和，但它们却为我们提出了一个需要做出的选择，或许也暗示了不同的承诺形式。

These two passages juxtapose the viewpoints that I’ve been trying to evoke in describing Gadamer’s position. The dignity and nobility of what Gadamer says is that it involves being interested in something “true,” keeping open the possibility that there could be a connection between meaning, arriving at meaning, and arriving at something that speaks to us as true. Hirsch, on the other hand, is evoking a completely different kind of dignity. What I want you to realize as we juxtapose these passages is that it is impossible to reconcile them, yet they pose for us a choice that needs to be made and perhaps suggests differing forms of commitment.

伽达默尔说（735；这里他又一次抨击了历史主义）：

Gadamer says (735; here again he’s attacking historicism):

从历史角度理解的文本，必然会放弃其声称自身表达真理的说法。我们以为，当我们从历史的角度看待过去，即把自己置于历史情境中并试图重构历史视野时，我们就理解了过去。然而，事实上，我们已经放弃了在过去中寻找任何对我们自身而言有效且可理解的真理的希望。
The text that is understood historically is forced to abandon its claim that it is uttering something true. We think we understand when we see the past from a historical standpoint, i.e., place ourselves in the historical situation and seek to reconstruct the historical horizon. In fact, however, we have given up the claim to find, in the past, any truth valid and intelligible for ourselves.

这种论点同样适用于文化对话。如果我为知道在另一种文化中，饭后打嗝是对厨师的赞美而感到自豪，但却不从中得出任何结论（除了“但在我来自的地方并非如此”），那就等同于历史主义。对我而言，这只是一个无关紧要的事实，而不是试图理解任何事物的努力。伽达默尔继续说道：“因此，这种对‘他者’的‘他者性’的承认，使他成为客观知识的对象，就意味着从根本上放弃了他关于真理的主张。”这是一个极具破坏性，而且我认为非常精辟的论点，它应该提醒我们，当我们倡导客观性时，我们究竟面临着怎样的风险。

This argument would also apply to cultural conversation. If I’m proud of knowing that in another culture when I belch after dinner it’s a compliment to the cook but draw no conclusions from this knowledge (other than “but not where I come from”), that would be the equivalent of historicism. It’s just a factoid for me, not an effort to come to terms with anything. Gadamer continues: “Thus, this acknowledgment of the otherness of the other, which makes him the object of objective knowledge, involves the fundamental suspension of his claim to truth.” This is a devastating and, I think, brilliant argument that ought to remind us of what’s at risk when we champion objectivity.

好了，现在听听赫希怎么说。这可不是个容易的选择。赫希援引康德的观点，指出：“康德认为，道德行为的基础在于，人应当被视为目的本身，而非他人的工具。”换句话说，只要我还在利用你、把你当成工具，你对我来说就只是手段而非目的。这就是康德的立场，而赫希正急于捍卫它。如果我认为自己无法理解某个实体作为目的本身的真正意义，那么我就是在为己谋利。这完全颠覆了我们应该对“他人所言为真”这一理念的根本。难道只有当它能教会我一些东西时，它才重要吗？

All right, but now listen to Hirsch. This isn’t an easy choice. What Hirsch says, rightly invoking Kant, is this: “Kant held it to be a foundation of moral action that men should be conceived as ends in themselves, not as instruments of other men.” In other words, you are a means and not an end to me as long as I’m exploiting you and instrumentalizing you. That’s Kant’s position, which Hirsch is leaping to defend. If I don’t think I can come to terms with the actual meaning of an entity as that entity, as an end in itself, I am appropriating it for my own benefit. This turns the whole idea of being open to the possibility that the other is speaking true upside-down. Does it matter only if it teaches me something?

赫希继续说道：

Hirsch continues:

这种要求同样适用于人的言语，因为言语是人在社会领域的延伸和表达，而且，当我们未能将人的意图与他的言语联系起来时，我们就失去了言语的灵魂，即传达意义和理解想要传达的内容。
This imperative is transferable to the words of men because speech is an extension and expression of men in the social domain and also because when we fail to conjoin a man’s intention to his words, we lose the soul of speech, which is to convey meaning and to understand what is intended to be conveyed.

值得注意的是，尽管这种高尚与伽达默尔的情感形成鲜明对比，其高尚之处显而易见，也让我们感到矛盾——然而，与伽达默尔不同，赫希并未谈论真理。他谈论的是意义的获取——这当然是件好事——并且他尽可能地使“获得正确意义”这一概念具有说服力，但关键在于，他并未谈论真理。对赫希而言，重要的是意义本身。对伽达默尔而言，重要的是意义的真实性，而这正是二者本质区别所在。由于伽达默尔相信先入之见的不可避免性，他愿意牺牲意义在历史或文化上的精确性。他说，我的诠释中总是带有“我”的印记，但他同时坚持认为，如果我不关注其他视角，诠释的循环就会陷入恶性循环。我不能说“塑料”就等于“聚合物”，但我需要记住，在我所处的教育环境中，只有我知道“塑料”曾经意味着不同的东西，而我对塑料特别感兴趣，正是因为它的含义发生了变化。

Notice that although the nobility of this in contrast with the nobility of Gadamer’s sentiment is obvious and makes us feel torn—notice, however, that unlike Gadamer, Hirsch is not saying anything about truth. He’s talking about securing meaning—which is surely a good thing—and he’s making the notion of arriving at a correct meaning as persuasive as he possibly can, but it remains significant that he’s not talking about truth. For Hirsch the important thing is the meaning. For Gadamer the important thing is that the meaning be true, and that’s where the distinction essentially lies. Because of his belief in the inescapability of preconception, Gadamer is willing to sacrifice historical or cultural exactitude of meaning. He says there’s always something of me in my interpretation, insisting, however, that the hermeneutic circle is a vicious one if I am not mindful of other horizons. I must not say that “plastic” means “polymer,” but I need to remember that it’s I, within my climate of education, who know that “plastic” once meant something different, and I who take a special interest in plastic precisely because its meaning has changed.

顺便说一句，说赫希漠视真理其实对他并不公平。当然，赫希很在意对方是否说真话（这也是他后来声称学童必须学习一套共同的核心真理的原因），但这种信念并非他在此段论述中所持哲学立场的内在体现。至少部分原因在于此，对于任何学者、任何读者而言，这都是一个必须在不可通约的事物之间做出的选择。这一选择贯穿于文学理论课程以及对文学理论传统的理解之中。今天我所阐述的这两种立场之间的区别，你们看到的还远未结束。

It is actually unfair to Hirsch, by the way, to say that he disregards truth. Certainly it matters to Hirsch whether the other speaks true (that’s why he has since said that schoolchildren must learn a common core of truths), but that conviction is not implicit in the philosophical position he takes up in this passage. At least in part for this reason, for any scholar, for any reader, this is a choice between incommensurables that really does have to be made. It’s a choice that looms over a course in literary theory and in coming to understand the tradition of literary theory. You have not seen anywhere near the last of the distinction between these two positions that I’ve been making today.

 

 

第四章

CHAPTER 4

配置阅读
Configurative Reading

阅读：

Reading:

伊瑟尔，沃尔夫冈。“阅读过程：现象学方法。”载于《批评传统》，第 1002-1014 页。

Iser, Wolfgang. “The Reading Process: A Phenomenological Approach.” In The Critical Tradition, pp. 1002–1014.

在本讲中，我们将继续探讨诠释学的方法。在进一步讨论E.D.赫希，并转向沃尔夫冈·伊瑟之前，我想回到伽达默尔，再谈谈他隐含的选书品味，以及他诠释学方法所建立的文学和思想经典。你们应该记得，伽达默尔关注的是古典主义的规范，在你们的摘录中，他后来开始称之为“传统”。对他而言，传统如此重要的原因与政治或文化保守主义者认为传统重要的原因并不完全相同；伽达默尔认为，读者理解遥远时空的能力是有限的。他不认为读者能够凭直觉感受到另一个时空的视角，从而创造奇迹；因此，古典主义或传统的价值在于，在我们称之为古典的文本中存在着显而易见的共同基础。有时我们称它们为“伟大的著作”，这类文本能够与所有时空对话，或者我们感觉它们似乎能够与所有时空对话。人们普遍质疑，在历史差异如此深远且有时难以调和的情况下，以这种方式讨论文本是否真的有意义。但目前我只想重申，伽达默尔对经典的保守态度源于他对读者能否跨越巨大鸿沟的怀疑。我特意在此使用“鸿沟”一词，因为沃尔夫冈·伊瑟在谈论读者与文本之间保持距离的优势，以及文本中连续段落之间的语义距离时，都赋予了这个词完全积极的意义，这一点我们稍后会看到。

In this lecture we continue discussing approaches to interpretation. Before we talk further about E. D. Hirsch and then move to Wolfgang Iser, I want to go back to Gadamer and say something more about his implied taste in books, about the kind of literary and intellectual canon that his approach to hermeneutics establishes. You remember that Gadamer is concerned with the norm of classicism, which later in your excerpt he begins to call “tradition.” The reason tradition is so important for him is not quite the same as the reason tradition is important for a political or cultural conservative; Gadamer thinks the reader has a limited capacity to understand a remote horizon. He doesn’t think the reader can perform miracles in intuitively feeling his or her way into the outlook of another time and place; hence the value of classicism, or tradition, is that there is evident common ground in the texts we call classical. Sometimes we refer to them as “great books,” the sorts of text that speak, or we feel as though they’re speaking, to all places and times. It’s widely contested whether there is really any merit in talking about texts that way when their historical differences remain so profound and sometimes so inassimilable, but for the moment I repeat only that Gadamer’s conservatism about the canon is related to his doubt about the ability of readers to span enormous gaps. I use that word “gaps” advisedly here because it is the word to which Wolfgang Iser attaches a wholly positive value in talking about the advantage of distance between the reader and the text and also about the semantic distance between successive moments of a text, as we’ll see.

伽达默尔是否低估了读者的思维跳跃能力？或许如此。在阐述这个问题的脚注（731）中，他提出了一个颇为奇特的观点：“正如在对话中一样，我们对反讽的理解程度取决于我们与对方在主题上的共识程度。”也就是说，如果你表达的观点与我的观点截然不同，伽达默尔认为我将无法理解你是否在反讽，或者如果你在反讽，你的反讽又意味着什么。在我看来，这显然是错误的。想想政治：政治脱口秀、政治竞选。当我们的政治对手反讽我们的观点时，我们完全能够理解其中的反讽。我们已经习以为常，我们已经适应了这种反讽，当然，我们的对手也理解我们的反讽。颇具讽刺意味的是，政治对手之间存在着一种共生关系，这种关系恰恰取决于他们彼此反讽的理解程度，而这无疑也适用于一般的对话。大多数讽刺形式都很容易解读，而且这种能力肯定不依赖于任何必要的、潜在的共识。

Does Gadamer underestimate the mental leaps of which readers are capable? Perhaps so. In a footnote elaborating on this question (731), he says something peculiar: “just as in conversation, we understand irony to the extent to which we are in agreement on the subject with the other person.” That is, if you are expressing an opinion that differs radically from my own, Gadamer thinks I will not be able to understand whether you’re being ironic, or what your irony means if you are. This seems to me just patently false. Think about politics: political talk shows, political campaigns. When our political opponent is being ironic about our views, we understand the irony perfectly well. We’re used to it, we have accommodated ourselves to it, and of course our opponent understands our ironies, too. There is a kind of symbiosis, ironically enough, between political opponents precisely in the measure to which their ironies are mutually intelligible, and surely this applies to conversation in general. It’s quite easy to decode most forms of irony, and this facility surely doesn’t depend on any necessary, underlying agreement.

如果我的想法没错，或许我们已经找到了伽达默尔关于读者思维弹性的保守主义中的一个漏洞。他的前提是，为了理解，必须存在共识的基础；但如果我们刚才所说的，即使存在分歧，我们也能理解彼此的讽刺之处，那么这也应该适用于我们阅读那些我们明显不认同的文本的能力，我们因此觉得永远无法肯定这些文本的价值，但我们仍然能够理解它们。因此，如果理解并非建立在共识之上，那么正如我们所说，“开放经典”的可能性——承认经典不必是连续的传统经典——就再次向我们敞开，而伽达默尔在这个问题上的保守主义也可以被搁置一旁。

Now if I’m right to think this, perhaps we have found a loophole in Gadamer’s conservatism about the elasticity of the reader’s mind. His premise is that in order to understand, there has to be a basis of agreement; but if what we’ve just said is true about understanding each other’s ironies even where there is disagreement, that ought to apply also to our capacity to read texts with which we distinctly disagree, the value of which we therefore feel we can never affirm but which we nevertheless can understand. Hence if understanding is not predicated on agreement, the possibility of “opening up the canon,” as we put it, conceding that it doesn’t have to be a continuous traditional canon, is available to us once again and Gadamer’s conservatism on this issue can be set aside.

然而，伽达默尔并非坚持绝对的连续性。恰恰相反。你或许还记得他在节选开头所说的话：为了意识到我们面对的某种表达或观念并不完全符合我们自身的历史视野，我们需要“突然醒悟”。换句话说，回到我们之前的例子，我们需要意识到阿肯赛德的“可塑性”一词存在某种怪异之处，而这种“突然醒悟”也让我们意识到阅读这一基本行为的必要性，伽达默尔称之为“视野的融合”。在这样的时刻，我们意识到自己面对的并非自身的视野，而只有与之协商，才能实现理解。

It’s not that Gadamer is insisting on absolute continuity, however. On the contrary. You’ll remember what he says early in the excerpt: in order to recognize that we are in the presence of an expression or idea that isn’t comfortably within our own historical horizon, we need to be “pulled up short.” In other words, to go back to our previous example, we need to recognize that there’s something weird about Akenside’s word “plastic,” and in being pulled up short we recognize the need also for the fundamental act of reading that Gadamer calls a merger of horizons. In such moments, we knowingly confront a horizon not our own that has to be negotiated if understanding is to take place.

我们也能做到这一点，伽达默尔也这么认为。事实上，他坚持认为，如果我们没有这种被突然拉回现实的体验，我们的阅读就会被束缚。我们会理所当然地认为，我们所读的内容完全属于我们自身的视野，而根本不会努力去理解那些本质上或至少在某些方面与我们视野相悖的事物。正如我所说，伽达默尔承认这一点，甚至坚持这一点，但他并没有着重强调，因为这种被突然拉回现实的需求所隐含的鸿沟并不大。我们很容易就能跨越它。再举个例子来说明“塑料”：如果我们不理解这个词在十八世纪的含义，我们仍然会注意到它的现代含义不合情理，所以我们会查阅《牛津英语词典》，发现它当时的含义不同，问题就解决了，然后我们就可以继续阅读。但是，在伽达默尔看来，可能还有其他一些情况会让我们感到被突然拉回现实，而这些情况超出了读者的想象力范围。正如我们将要讨论伊瑟尔时所看到的，这正是伽达默尔与伊瑟尔之间的根本区别，伊瑟尔在某些方面仍然是伽达默尔的追随者。对伽达默尔而言，读者与文本之间、我的视野与文本视野之间的差距必然很小；而对伊瑟尔而言，这种差距必须大得多，他所谓的“读者行为”，即阅读行为，才能真正发挥其作用。我们将看到，这种差异解释了他们各自隐含的规范之间的明显区别。

And we can do it, too, even according to Gadamer. In fact, he insists that if we don’t have this experience of being pulled up short, our reading is imprisoned. We just take it for granted that what we’re reading belongs exclusively to our own horizon and we don’t make any effort at all to understand what is fundamentally or at least in some ways alien to it. Gadamer acknowledges this, even insists on it as I say, but he doesn’t lay stress on it because the gap that is implied in the need to be pulled up short is not a big one. We can easily traverse it. Just to belabor the example of “plastic”: if we don’t understand the eighteenth-century meaning of the word, we still notice that the modern meaning is implausible, so we go to the Oxford English Dictionary, we see it meant something different then, our problem is solved, and we continue to read. But there may be other occasions for being pulled up short that in Gadamer’s view exceed the imaginative grasp of a reader. As you’ll see when we turn to Iser, this is the fundamental difference between Gadamer and Iser, who remains in some ways Gadamer’s disciple. Where for Gadamer the gap between reader and text, between my horizon and the horizon of the text, must be perforce a small one, for Iser it needs to be a much larger one in order for what he calls the “act of the reader,” the reading act, really to swing into high gear, and we’ll see that this difference accounts for the obvious difference between their two implied canons.

然而，此时我想讨论一下我们在上一讲结尾引用的赫希的其他段落（参见附录）。关于那段文字，简单回顾一下，大家应该记得伽达默尔说过，如果我们希望过去对我们“说真话”，就不能试图压抑我们自身的视角来理解过去的差异。如果我们只是简单地将自己的感受排除在外，这是不可能的，所以我们应该把阅读看作是一场积极的对话。另一方面，赫希借用康德的观点，认为过去的、文化背景迥异的作者应该是我们理解他们的目的，而不是手段，所以我们应该严格按照他们自身的视角来理解他们。

At this point, however, I want to discuss the other passages by Hirsch that we cited at the end of the last lecture (see also the appendix). As to that passage, quickly to review, you remember Gadamer said that we must not try to suppress our own outlook in approaching the otherness of the past if we wish the past to “speak true” to us. If we simply bracket out our own feelings, that can’t possibly happen, so we are enjoined to think of reading as an active conversation. Hirsch argues, on the other hand, borrowing from Kant, that past and culturally disparate authors should be an end and not a means for us, so we ought to understand them strictly on their terms.

我当时是在那种语境下介绍赫希的，现在我想简要地再谈谈他。首先是赫希的一个论点，我在上一讲也提到过，那就是“意义是意识的产物，而非文字的产物”。换句话说，文本使我们能够辨识意义，但意义本身并不存在于文本之中。意义属于作者的意图，而这正是我们在解读文本时需要达到的目标。我们必须将纸上的文字与作者的意识联系起来。

I introduced Hirsch in that context, then, and now I want to go back to him briefly. First there is Hirsch’s argument, also mentioned in the last lecture, that “meaning is an affair of consciousness and not of words.” In other words, the text is what makes the ascertainment of meaning available to us, but meaning is not in the text. Meaning belongs to the intention of the author, and that is what we need to arrive at as we work through the text. We must refer the words on the page to an authorial consciousness.

换句话说，我们用语言表达来指代某种思想。正如赫希在《诠释的目的》一书中论述的那样，这意味着在理解文本时，我们应该尝试用释义的方式来把握它。我们的回应可能以这样的方式开始：“作者想表达的是……” 因此，我们并不直接探究文本的含义。希尔施认为，如果仅从文本本身来看，这句话可能意味着任何事情：“我没油了”可能意味着“我冲出了一团氩气”。我们应该努力去发现作者“想要表达的意思”。

To put it another way, we refer a verbal expression to a thought. What this means, as Hirsch argues in a book called The Aims of Interpretation, is that in understanding a text we should attempt to grasp it in paraphrase. The beginning of our response might go something like: “What the author means to say is …” Hence we do not look for what the text meansit might mean anything, according to Hirsch, if you appeal to the text alone: “I ran out of gas” could mean “I raced out of a cloud of argon.” Rather we should attempt to discover what the author “means to say.”

人们很容易认为这完全是无稽之谈。在这种情况下，我们使用一份真实且触手可及的文本，去从充其量只是虚拟的、我们根本无法获取的东西中寻找意义？为什么我们不直接在文本中寻找意义呢？那样岂不是更合理？我们别无选择，只能解读文本。我们不可能知道作者的本意，除非我们根据文本中词语的含义来判断，那么为什么不直接将注意力集中在这种含义上呢？如果我们诉诸语境——除非是在某种可以想象的科幻语境中——“我从一团氩气中冲了出来”这句话同样不合情理，即便我们诉诸作者的意图也是如此。赫希是《意图谬误》的作者温萨特的学生，但显然他是一位叛逆者，这一点我们在讨论温萨特时就会看到。希尔施部分地受到温萨特的影响，坚持认为诉诸意图是唯一能够确立——正如他的第一本重要的诠释学著作的标题所言—— “解释的有效性”的方法。

It’s tempting to say that this is just absolute total nonsense. We use a text in that case, which is actual and ready to hand, to find meaning in something at best virtual, something we don’t have available to us? Why don’t we just find meaning in the text? That would make more sense. We have no choice but to construe the text. We can’t possibly know what the author meant except on the basis of our determination of the sense of the words in the text, so why not just focus our attention on that sense as its meaning? “I raced out of a cloud of argon” is just as implausible if we appeal to verbal context—except perhaps an imaginable science fiction context—as if we appeal to the intention of an author. Hirsch was a student of W. K. Wimsatt, the author of “The Intentional Fallacy,” but obviously a rebellious one, as we’ll see when we turn to Wimsatt. Thinking in part of Wimsatt, Hirsch insisted that appealing to intention is the only thing you can do in order to establish—according to the title of his first important book on hermeneutics—“validity in interpretation.”

因此，凭直觉很难认同赫希的观点，顺便一提，我也不认同，原因会在后续的讲座中逐渐阐明；但我必须为赫希辩护，如果我们仔细思考这个问题，就会意识到，在许多实际应用中，我们确实可以通过释义来判断作者的意图。例如，你们都听过老师在考试前叮嘱：“不要只是鹦鹉学舌地重复你所学习的作者的话。我希望你们真正理解这些作者。”想想看。你向老师证明你理解作者的方式，就是用不同的语言表达他们的意思。这样，你描述的是作者的意图，而不仅仅是文本的内容——如果你把考试变成一长串的引文，就可能证明这一点。老师想要的是解释，而不是引用，而解释的形式就是释义。除非你能找到一种人际意义，一种能被理解它并能用其他语言表达出来的群体所共享的意义，否则就无法进行释义。赫希认为，如果你能用其他语言表达作者的文字，那么这些其他语言就能确保传达作者的本意，即作者的思想。

It’s very difficult, then, intuitively to assent to Hirsch’s position, and I’ll just let you know by the way that I don’t, for reasons that will accumulate as these lectures continue; but I will say in defense of Hirsch that if we reflect on the matter, we must realize that for a great many practical purposes we do establish meaning as authorial intent through the test of paraphrase. For example, you’ve all heard your instructors tell you before you take an exam: “Don’t just parrot the words of the authors you’re studying. I want to know that you understand those authors.” Think about it. You prove to your teacher that you understand the authors by being able to put their meaning in other words. In this way, you describe the author’s intended meaning, not just what the text says, which you could demonstrate by making your exam one long quotation. The instructor wants explanation, not quotation, and the form of explanation is paraphrase. You can’t have paraphrase unless you can identify a meaning that is interpersonal, a meaning that can be shared among a group that understands it and can express it in other words. What Hirsch argues is that if you can put an author’s words in other words, those other words will secure the intended meaning, the author’s thought.

我认为，这是赫希一个相当重要的论点，但即便如此，我们仍然面临一个异议：正如我们已经指出的，我们总是用“换句话说”来描述意义。“我冲出了氩云”可能就是“我没油了”的意思，也可能不是，无论我们诉诸文本的意义还是作者的意义，但无论如何，它都是一种释义。然而，有一点我们可以承认（当我们考虑是否存在话语的“指称对象”时，这一点至关重要）：我们需要意识到，实际上，为了确保相互理解而诉诸释义的必要性，确实预设了意义是被指称的思想。

That’s a rather important argument in Hirsch’s favor, I think, yet even on this point an objection occurs to us: as we’ve already indicated, we always describe meaning “in other words.” “I raced out of an argon cloud” may or may not be the meaning of “I ran out of gas” no matter whether we appeal to the sense of a text or the meaning of an author, but it is a paraphrase in either case. This much, however, we can concede (and it will matter to have done so when we come to consider whether there is any such thing as a “referent” for an utterance): we need to realize that, practically speaking, the necessity of appealing to paraphrase in order to guarantee mutual understanding certainly does entail presupposing that meaning is a referred-to thought.

一门文学理论课程必然会揭示释义在严谨的阐释任务中存在的不足，所以——再次声明——我现在就不多赘述了。克林斯·布鲁克斯（Cleanth Brooks）是一位新批评家，也是希尔施的导师温萨特（Wimsatt）的批评盟友。他曾写过一篇题为《释义的异端邪说》的文章，希尔施无疑也对此有所思考。布鲁克斯坚持认为，如果将文本表面的复杂性简化为释义，那么文学阐释就成了一种僵化、机械、缺乏灵活性的行为。关于释义的问题，我暂且就此打住。

A course of lectures on literary theory will inevitably show the ways in which paraphrase is inadequate to the task of rigorous interpretation, so—again—I won’t say much about it now. Cleanth Brooks, a New Critic and critical ally of Hirsch’s mentor Wimsatt, had written an essay called “The Heresy of Paraphrase,” no doubt also on Hirsch’s mind, insisting that literary interpretation is a wooden, mechanical, inflexible exercise if it reduces the complexity of a textual surface to paraphrase. And there I’ll leave the question of paraphrase for the moment.

希尔施在我之前提到的另一段文字中论证道——我现在来转述一下！——伽达默尔未能理解文本的意义和文本的重要性之间的区别。这是希尔施的另一个关键观点，我们可以这样理解：文本的意义是作者意图表达的意思，我们可以通过可靠的转述来确定这一点。文本的重要性（希尔施并不否认其重要性）是指文本对我们而言的意义——例如，我们如何从历史的角度将其转化为我们自己的理解，或者如何将其应用于某种事业或某种思想观点。希尔施坚持认为——当然，他的区分也正是在这里引发了争议——意义和重要性是可以区分的。如果你们这些优秀的史学家能够准确、无可争议地确定作者的意思，诉诸所有可用的语文学证据，剔除无关因素，并确信自己最终理解了正确的意思，那么，一旦你们做到了这一点，你们就可以对文本赋予任何你们想要的意义。

Hirsch argues in another passage I’ve given you—I’ll paraphrase now!—that Gadamer fails to realize the difference between the meaning of a text and the significance of a text. This is Hirsch’s other key position, and we can understand it as follows: The meaning of a text is what the author intended it to mean, which we can establish with a reliable paraphrase. The significance of the text, to which Hirsch does not deny interest, is the meaning for us—the way in which, for example, we can translate it into our own terms historically or can adapt it to a cause or to an intellectual outlook. Hirsch insists—and here, of course, is where his distinction becomes controversial—that it’s possible to tell the difference between meaning and significance. If, good historicists that you may be, you can pin down accurately and incontestably the author’s meaning, appealing to all the philological evidence available, throwing out irrelevancies, and becoming convinced that you finally have the meaning right, then, once you’ve done that, you can impose any sort of significance on the text that you wish.

伽达默尔并未对这一区别发表评论，但他肯定不会同意我们能够可靠地区分意义和重要性。因为进入诠释学循环的正确且必要的途径是达到视域的融合——既包括我们自身的视域，也包括文本的视域——所以我们无法清晰地知道意义的终点和重要性的起点。就定义而言，赫希的区分本身足够清晰，甚至颇具启发性。然而，要在实践中真正确立这一区分，即声称你理解了作者的意义，并且现在能够以一种完全不同的方式解释这个意义对你而言为何具有重要意义——这无疑是一项壮举。

Gadamer does not comment on the distinction, but he certainly would not agree that we can distinguish between meaning and significance with any reliability. Because the proper and necessary way into the hermeneutic circle is to arrive at a merger of horizons, our own horizon and the horizon of the text, we cannot know with clarity where meaning leaves off and significance begins. As a matter of definition, Hirsch’s distinction is in itself clear enough and even rather bracing. Yet to secure the distinction in actual practice, to say that you know the author’s meaning and will now, in a wholly distinct gesture, explain how the meaning is significant for you—well, that would be a feat.

接下来我们来谈谈沃尔夫冈·伊瑟尔：这位理论家关注的是他所谓的“读者行为”，或者说“阅读行为”——《阅读行为》（Der Akt des Lesens）是他的一本书的书名——他以此为重点，加入了源于胡塞尔的现象学传统，而就伊瑟尔而言，更直接地，他受到了波兰学者罗曼·英加登的影响。英加登是一位分析读者在文本中逐句阅读的学者，你读过的那篇文章中也多次引用了他的观点。（伊瑟尔正是参照英加登的观点，谈到了句子思维与句子思维之间的“鸿沟”，而英加登并不认同这种鸿沟——也就是说，他指的是句子思维与句子思维之间的鸿沟，而不是文本与读者之间的鸿沟。）这些学者，连同伽达默尔，是伊瑟尔的主要思想来源，而伊瑟尔反过来也对其他人产生了巨大的影响。他对读者体验的关注，促成了20世纪60年代和70年代康斯坦茨大学一个思想流派的形成，并由此开设了一系列关于“接受史”或“接受美学”的研讨会。伊瑟在康斯坦茨的同事之一是汉斯·罗伯特·尧斯，我们稍后会讨论他。所谓的康斯坦茨学派的影响扩展到了美国，并在这里产生了诸多影响，尤其体现在另一位批评家斯坦利·菲什的早期著作中，我们将在本书后面部分讨论到他。

Turning then to Wolfgang Iser: this theorist is concerned with what he calls the act of the reader, or of reading—Der Akt des Lesens is the title of one of his books—and with this emphasis he joins the tradition of phenomenology deriving from Husserl and more directly, in Iser’s case, from an analyst of the way in which the reader moves from sentence to sentence in negotiating a text, the Polish scholar Roman Ingarden, who is quoted frequently in the essay you’ve read. (It is with Ingarden in mind that Iser speaks of the “gaps,” of which Ingarden does not approve, between sentence-thought and sentence-thought—not, that is, the gaps between text and reader.) Those writers together with Gadamer are the primary influences on Iser, who has been tremendously influential in turn. His interest in the reader’s experience helped found a school of thought at the University of Konstanz in the 1960s and 1970s, resulting in a series of seminars on what was called “reception history” or, alternatively, “the aesthetics of reception.” One of Iser’s Konstanz colleagues was Hans Robert Jauss, whom we will be discussing eventually. The influence of the so-called Konstanz School spread to the United States and had many ramifications here, especially in the early work of another critic we’ll be turning to later in this book, Stanley Fish.

接受史既是一个理论性强、又具有学术性的领域，近年来在“书籍史”和媒体接受研究等运动中依然蓬勃发展。伊瑟尔在其职业生涯后期，每年都在加州大学欧文分校任教。那时，他正致力于研究其项目的一个新方向，他称之为“小说人类学”，探讨我们为何拥有小说以及我们为何彼此讲述故事等根本问题。伊瑟尔的所有研究都基于文学即虚构的理念。他几乎完全是一位小说学者。事实上，伊瑟尔与伽达默尔的一个重要区别在于，伽达默尔是一位思想史学家，其经典文本涵盖哲学著作、社会思想著作和古典文学作品，而伊瑟尔始终是一位文学叙事研究者。

Reception history has been a partly theoretical, partly scholarly field, one that’s still flourishing in recent movements, such as “the history of the book” and the study of media reception. Later in his career, Iser taught annually at the University of California, Irvine, and by that time he was pursuing a new aspect of his project that he called the anthropology of fiction, posing the fundamental questions of why we have fiction and why we tell stories to each other. All of Iser’s work is grounded in the notion of literature as fiction. He’s almost exclusively a scholar of the novel. In fact, an important difference between Iser and Gadamer is that whereas Gadamer is an intellectual historian whose canonical texts are works of philosophy, works of social thought, and classical works of literature, Iser has always been a student of literary narrative.

尽管存在这些差异，但当你阅读伊瑟尔的作品时，你会发现，无论从语气还是他对我们如何解读文本世界的理解来看，他都更接近伽达默尔而非赫希。我们可以从两个方面来阐述这一点。首先，伊瑟尔重构了伽达默尔关于视域融合的论述——而赫希则否定了这一论述。例如，他写道（1002）：“文本与读者的融合使文学作品得以存在。”伽达默尔会谈到读者视域与文本呈现的视域的融合。“融合”、“融合”：并非文本的视域，也并非读者的视域；而是当这些视域融合时所产生的有效历史，这构成了“作品”——一部分是他人的作品，一部分是读者的作品。这相当于说意义的空间是“虚拟的”——伊瑟尔用这个词来解释：“这种融合永远无法被精确地指出，而必须始终保持虚拟状态，既不能与文本的现实性等同，也不能与读者的个人倾向等同。”

Yet despite these differences, you’ll see as you read Iser that in tone and in his understanding of the way we negotiate the world of texts he much more closely resembles Gadamer than Hirsch. We can put this in two different ways. We can say for one thing that Iser reconstructs what Gadamer says—and Hirsch denies—about the merger of horizons. For example, he says (1002), “The convergence of text and reader brings the literary work into existence.” Gadamer would speak of the merger of the reader’s horizon with the horizon within which the text appears. “Convergence,” “merger”: It’s not the text’s horizon; it’s not the reader’s horizon; it’s the effective history that takes place when those horizons merge that constitutes the “work”—partly someone else’s work, partly the reader’s. This amounts to saying that the space of meaning is “virtual”—the word Iser uses: “[A]nd this convergence can never be precisely pinpointed, but must always remain virtual, and is not to be identified either with the reality of the text or with the individual disposition of the reader.”

此外，伊瑟显然与伽达默尔一样坚信，意义的建构不可能完全客观。他并不比伽达默尔更倾向于历史主义，而是强调这两个视角之间存在着偏见的相互交流（1005）：“一个文本可能存在多种不同的解读，任何解读都无法穷尽其全部潜力，因为每个读者都会以自己的方式填补空白。” “空白”一词再次展现了其趣味性。我并不确定伊瑟——借用赫希的观点——是否也像我接下来要说的那样理解“空白”，但除了指代有限宽度的开口之外，“空白”一词也让人联想到火花塞。火花塞中的电流要正常工作，两个接触点之间必须存在“间隙”。它们必须被拉开到一定程度，但又不能太远。间隙过大，则无法产生火花；间隙过小，则会导致短路，同样无法产生火花。在我看来，阅读的“顿悟”效应，即读者与文本之间来回穿梭的体验，可以理解为读者与文本之间的关系就像火花塞上两个触点之间的关系。

In addition, Iser plainly shares with Gadamer the conviction that the construal of meaning cannot be altogether objective. He is no more of a historicist than Gadamer is but insists rather on the mutual exchange of prejudice between the two horizons in question (1005): “One text is potentially capable of several different realizations, and no reading can ever exhaust the full potential, for each individual reader will fill in the gaps in his own way.” “Gaps,” again, is an interesting term. I don’t actually know whether Iser—to be Hirschian—means what I’m about to say about gaps, but apart from designating openings of finite width, “gaps” also call spark plugs to mind. For the electrical current to operate in a spark plug, the two points of contact have to be “gapped.” They have to be forced apart to a certain degree but not too far. Too much, there’s no spark. Too little, you short out and there’s no spark. It seems to me, then, that the “ah-ha” effect of reading, the movement back and forth across the gap between the reader and the text, can be understood as though the relationship between the reader and the text were the relationship between the two points of a spark plug.

那么，伊瑟与伽达默尔有何不同呢？鉴于我们刚才对赫希的论述，有一点不同之处值得关注；此外，还有一点至关重要的不同之处，我们之前已经提到过，需要再次提及。首先，伊瑟似乎区分了“阅读”和“阐释”（1006）： “文本直接指向我们自身的先入之见”——伽达默尔称之为“偏见”——“这些先入之见通过阐释行为而显露出来，而阐释行为是阅读过程的基本要素。” 这句话中在阅读和阐释之间划出了一条界限，这似乎类似于赫希在意义和重要性之间划出的界限。意义或阅读是建构；重要性或阐释则是对这种建构的应用。然而，伊瑟并没有过多地强调这一区别，因此，在这方面，他与伽达默尔的分歧并不大。

How then does Iser differ from Gadamer? There is one point of difference that is interesting in view of what we’ve just been saying about Hirsch, and there’s another crucial point of difference, mentioned already, to which we need to return. First, then, Iser actually seems to distinguish (1006) between “reading” and “interpretation”: “[T]he text refers back directly to our own preconceptions”—Gadamer would call those “prejudices”—“which are revealed by the act of interpretation that is a basic element of the reading process.” There’s a wedge in this sentence between reading and interpretation that seems to resemble the wedge Hirsch drives between meaning and significance. Meaning or reading is construal; significance or interpretation is the application of that construal. Iser doesn’t make much of the distinction, however, so in this respect his divergence from Gadamer is slight.

然而，另一个分歧却是伊瑟思想的核心。回到这一点，伊瑟强调创新是指导阅读阐释策略的价值原则。创新正是伊瑟的经典体系所珍视的，也正是这一点使其与伽达默尔的连续传统经典体系截然不同。伊瑟对“火花塞间隙”的理解大胆地肯定了读者的想象力。为了说明伊瑟所谓的“虚拟工作”是如何实现的，我快速地引用几段文字。伽达默尔曾说过（但并未着重强调），为了意识到自身视野与文本视野之间的差异，你需要“突然醒悟”，需要感到惊讶；而伊瑟则将全部精力都放在了这种惊讶感上。如果不能带来惊讶，就没有价值，就会像批评家和伊瑟本人居高临下地称之为“烹饪式”——过于熟悉，如同例行公事。如果惊喜元素要在阅读过程中发挥关键作用，那么这种差距就必须拉大到极致，而这正是伊瑟尔在我即将快速引用的段落中所表达的意思。

The other divergence, though, is central to Iser’s thought. To return, then, to this point, Iser stresses innovation as the principle of value governing the interpretive strategies of reading. Innovation is what Iser’s canon values, and that’s what makes it so different from Gadamer’s continuous traditional canon. Iser’s understanding of gapping the spark plug boldly affirms the imaginative powers of the reader. In order to illustrate how what Iser calls “virtual work” gets done in this regard, let me just run through a few passages quickly. Whereas Gadamer says, again, but without emphasis, that in order to become aware that there is a difference between your own horizon and the horizon of the text you need to be “pulled up short,” to be surprised, Iser throws his whole emphasis on this element of surprise. If it doesn’t surprise, it doesn’t have value, it’s what critics and Iser himself condescendingly call “culinary”—overly familiar like routine cooking. If the element of surprise is to play its key role in the reading process, the gap has to stretch to the utmost, and that’s what Iser is saying in the passages I’m about to quote rapid-fire.

“在这个创造过程中”——即文本引发读者惊喜感的方式——“文本可能不够深入，也可能过犹不及”（1003）。诚然，在这段话中，我们能感受到一丝伽达默尔的保守主义倾向。文本可能“过犹不及”，对我们提出过高的要求。《芬尼根守灵夜》就给一些读者留下了这样的印象。我们无法流畅地阅读句子，甚至在同一句子中，我们也完全不明白字里行间的意思。许多读者确实热情地接受了这种挑战；但用伊瑟的话来说，这类文本至少冒着过犹不及的风险。正如伊瑟所说：“我们可以说，厌倦和过度紧张构成了读者离开阅读领域的界限。”如果没有惊喜，阅读文本就毫无意义。如果惊喜太多，就会造成过度紧张，最终导致我们沮丧地扔掉这本书。

“In this process of creativity”—the way in which a text induces the feeling of surprise in the reader—“the text may either not go far enough, or may go too far” (1003). In this particular passage, admittedly, you get a hint of Gadamer’s conservatism. The text may “go too far,” making demands on us that are too great. Finnegans Wake strikes some readers this way. We can’t get from sentence to sentence, and even within a sentence we have no idea what the words mean. Many readers do enthusiastically meet the challenge; but in Iser’s terms this sort of text has at least risked going too far. Again: “[W]e may say that boredom and overstrain form the boundaries beyond which the reader will leave the field of play.” If there are no surprises, there’s no point in reading the text. If the surprises are too great, they induce overstrain and we throw the book away in frustration.

伊瑟尔说：“在真正的文学文本中，期望几乎从未得到满足”（1004）。“期望”在伊瑟尔所描述的阅读过程中，调节着诠释学的循环。根据伊瑟尔的观点，阅读的本质在于打破期望。然而，为了弥补这种摆脱可预测性的自由，在句子之间，必须有一种感觉，即接下来可能会发生什么，无论那是什么。如果这种潜在的感觉不存在，那么无论发生什么，都只会令人沮丧；但如果我们期望接下来会发生什么，而结果却并非如此，那反而是一件好事。这就是彻底颠覆伽达默尔隐含经典的评价原则。在文学文本中，价值的赋予或确立，并非连续性，而是创新，是打破期望的期望。我们感受到的不是真理在深渊的另一边向我们诉说；我们感受到的，是深渊的另一边，我们正在经历建设性的惊喜。

“[E]xpectations,” says Iser, “are scarcely ever fulfilled in a truly literary text” (1004). “Expectations” mediate the hermeneutic circle as it applies to the reading process Iser describes. Reading consists, according to Iser, in the violation of expectations. Yet to offset this freedom from the predictable, there has to be a sense, moving from sentence to sentence, that something is likely to happen next, whatever it may be. If that underlying sense isn’t there, then whatever happens is simply met with frustration, but if we have the expectation that something’s going to happen next, and then something different happens, that’s all to the good. This is the evaluative principle that completely revolutionizes Gadamer’s implied canon. Not continuity but innovation, the expectation of violated expectation, is what imposes or establishes value in the literary text. We don’t sense that across the abyss truth is being spoken to us; we sense rather that across the abyss we are being constructively surprised.

当伊瑟尔提到“阐释性文本”时，他或许是在暗指伽达默尔，后者主要指的是阐释性文本：这类哲学和社会思想作品并非试图出其不意或欺骗读者，而是力求构建一个连贯一致的论证，尽可能减少意外。哲学和社会思想本身就很难，但难点不在于出其不意，而在于其词汇和思想的复杂性。伊瑟尔也承认这一点：“我们其实默认要求阐释性文本……在阐述其要呈现的对象时，不应有任何意外——但这却是文学文本的缺陷。” 这就是伊瑟尔眼中非虚构作品与虚构作品的区别。

When Iser does mention “expository texts,” he may be alluding to Gadamer, who has expository texts chiefly in mind: works of philosophy and social thought that aren’t trying to surprise or trick us but trying instead to lay out an argument that is consistent and continuous, keeping surprise to a minimum. It’s difficult, philosophy and social thought, but it’s not difficult because of the element of surprise. It’s the vocabulary and the complexity of the thought that make it difficult. Iser acknowledges this: “[W]e implicitly demand of expository texts … [that there be no surprise] as we refer to the objects they are meant to present—[but it’s] a defect in a literary text.” Here is the difference for Iser between nonfiction and fiction.

当我们探讨俄国形式主义者时，很快就会遇到“陌生化”这个词。“陌生化”的确切含义是，它会让你措手不及，让你感到你原本以为会发生的事或你以为的现状并非事实。诗人华莱士·史蒂文斯对此做了精辟的阐述，他说诗歌应该“让可见之物变得难以辨认”；换句话说，它应该使那些已经变得过于熟悉和可预测的事物变得陌生。伊瑟尔正是针对阅读过程的这一方面指出：“读者自以为熟悉的事物的陌生化必然会产生一种张力，这种张力既会加剧他的预期，也会加剧他对这些预期的怀疑”（1010）。

The word “defamiliarization” we will encounter soon when we take up the Russian formalists. “Defamiliarization” means, precisely, pulling you up short or taking you by surprise, making you feel that what you thought was going to be the case or what you thought was the state of affairs is not the state of affairs. The poet Wallace Stevens puts it beautifully when he says that poetry should “make the visible a little hard to see”; in other words, it should defamiliarize that which has become too familiar and predictable. It is to this aspect of the reading process that Iser refers in saying: “[The] defamiliarization of what the reader thought he recognized is bound to create a tension that will intensify his expectations as well as his distrust of those expectations” (1010).

这种论断至少部分地将价值转移到了所谓的阅读心理学上。阅读需要一种张力：既抱有期待，又感觉这些期待应该被打破，而且很可能会被打破，同时还要时刻警惕这些期待将如何被打破。在伊瑟看来，这种张力正是阅读带来的心理兴奋点。简而言之，伊瑟认为健康的读者应该努力阅读，放弃放松。如果文本看起来只是真实存在，没有对日常生活进行任何修饰，也没有意识到这是一个虚构的世界，那么阅读就缺乏足够的努力。在这种情况下，两者之间的差距不够大。作为对阅读内容的一种隐含评价，这种说法值得商榷。小说史反复青睐那些力求与现实完全一致的虚构世界。可以说，乔纳森·弗兰岑的小说之所以广受欢迎，正是因为如此。打破期待并非这类小说的驱动力。伊瑟尔可能没有考虑到另一种心理上的愉悦，那就是模仿带来的愉悦，正如亚里士多德所说，这种愉悦会让我们惊呼：“啊，那就是他。”

This pronouncement transfers value at least in part to what might be called the psychology of reading. Reading requires the tension of simultaneously having expectations and feeling that they should be violated, that probably they will be violated, and being on the alert for how they’re going to be violated.
